Many Canadians who have lost faith in our political system and its
leadership want to change not only the politicians who represent them, but our system of government as well.
Our present Canadian parliamentary system that has existed for 150 years is based on the union of the executive and the legislative branches of government. This means that every cabinet minister must have a seat in one of the Houses of Parliament and in theory at least that the cabinet as a whole is responsible to the House of Commons. In practice, however, the House of Commons is now actually responsible to the cabinet since the Commons enacts only legislation chosen by the cabinet within time limits set by the cabinet.
If we are to restore Canadians' faith in our political system, we must not only ensure that MPs reflect the views of those they are elected to represent, but also that the cabinet is responsible to those MPs in practice as well as in theory.

Mr. Speaker, last week was the anniversary of the storming of the Gold Temple in Amritsar.
June 4 to June 7 will stay in the memory of Sikhs throughout the world for generations to come. The desecration of the holiest shrine in Sikhism was a devastating event for Sikhs in Canada.
We share the grief of the Sikh community on the seventh anniversary of Operation Blue Star, the Indian government's code name for the storming of the Gold Temple.

Sikhs all over the world will never forget these events, this assault on their identity and their spirit. I share the memory of these tragic events with the Sikh community, and I hope all members will join me in commemorating that day.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to inform the House that Senator David Croll passed away yesterday, and I would like to pay tribute to a great Canadian.
This man devoted all his life to public life. He was from a minority group and had to struggle in the 1930s to get elected. He managed to attain very high offices in our land. He was Mayor of Windsor. He was the first person of the Jewish faith to become a member of the Ontario cabinet and the first one to become a senator.
I had the privilege to serve in the caucus of the Liberal Party with Senator Croll for more than a quarter of a centuiy. He was an extremely impressive person. Senator Croll had only one preoccupation and it was to defend those who were defenceless in our society. It was to fight for those who needed the help of other Canadians. He was a promoter of all the social programs that we are so proud of today, and he had been a promoter of these programs since the 1920s and 1930s.
Senator Croll always said that in a country like Canada nobody should go to bed hungry, nobody should be homeless, nobody should suffer, because there is enough in this country to provide a decent living for any human being.

Senator Croll was one of those reformers who left their mark on this country. He was elected to public office as a very young man. He was mayor, minister and senator. However, the focus of his contribution was always to defend the rights of the neediest in our society.
As a political party, there have been times when we were unsure about the path we should take and every time we had doubts, when the Liberal Party was somewhat disoriented, Senator Croll would rise and tell us what to do. One of his principles was always to give the weakest members of our society the benefit of the doubt. He was a great Liberal. He was a great teacher for us all

June 12, 1991

in this House. I think his sudden departure will be a great loss not only for my party but for the Senate and the entire country as well. There have been very few politicians of his moral calibre.

There is nothing Canada cannot do and do best. We have to do it when we can stand proud, remembering that there are those who have received less and those who have been put aside because of either faith, colour, sex or other differences because in Canada we are all equal.
What is important in human beings is always the human being itself. David Croll had almost been a father to me and many others, because whenever we were in doubt, and I was many times in my career, we asked David Croll what to do.
He always said: "You have to be on the side of those who need help, on the side of justice and dignity". This man has made a great mark on Canada, and I would like to offer his family our condolences. I hope there will be many more David Crolls in Canadian society in the years to come.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too would like to pay tribute to Senator David Croll on behalf of my party and on behalf of those of us in my community in Toronto who were admirers of the late senator.

Let me join the hon. Leader of the Opposition in hoping that there will be many more of his stature who will choose to serve in public life.

I remember when I was first elected to this House and after being here a couple of years, in 1971 he issued a report on poverty. He was the chairman of the Senate Committee on Poverty. His report was very revealing about the situation at that time. It made many recommendations about helping poor people in this country.
He was a man of tremendous dedication to a cause. It is important that we think of Senator Croll and remember in him that he had a cause. He had a purpose to be in public life, and he was in public life in many different capacities.
He started as mayor of Windsor in 1930. Later he became a member of the provincial parliament in Ontario. He was a cabinet minister with two or three different portfolios and in 1945 he was a member of Parliament for the federal riding of Toronto-Spadina. In 1955 he was appointed as a senator for the province of Ontario.

He was a great Canadian and a great democrat. He was an example to all of us here in the House, to those in the other place and to all Canadians.
On behalf of my party I wish to offer my condolences to his family and friends.

speakerposition: Bloc Québécois House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the 10 years or more that I was in the Liberal caucus, there were certain people who made an impression on us, and I think Senator David Croll was one of those people. Few politicians are perpetual idealists. Many of us become cynical over time, but I believe Senator Croll was a perpetual idealist. He had not the slightest trace of opportunism or political self-interest. He always acted according to his principles, especially where defending human dignity was concerned. Very few politicians earn the respect of all members of this House. I think Senator Croll led the way for many of us who believe in philosophy and human dignity. I wish to extend our condolences to his family, and I hope he will remain a guide for us all.

June 12, 1991
Tributes

Mr. Speaker, I would like to say what an immense privilege it has been for me to have been in Parliament and in the Liberal caucus with David Croll.
I will not review in detail the highlights of his career. Others have done that. Certainly we will be hearing more in the coming days.
I would like to mention that in 1971 at the age of 71 he chaired the Senate Committee on Poverty and recommended the implementation of a guaranteed annual income for all families and individuals. He said later it is the only way to give people the minimum living standards to which they are entitled.
What I really want to talk about is what it was like to hear David Croll speak. He was a gentle man with a sparkle in his eye. He spoke softly, but with such power. Every time he spoke, the room would fall silent. People would listen because they knew that he had something important to say. He always spoke about the needs of the elderly, the poor, the sick and how we had an obligation to respond to their interests.

I had a special affinity to and affection for David Croll. He was born on March 12, 1900, at the turn of the century, and my father was born on January 1, 1900. There was a certain similarity in the way they talked.

I would like to express my sympathies to the members of Senator Croll's family. We will remember him for a long, long, long time and we will honour ourselves if we can dedicate ourselves to fight for the ideals and the principles that David Croll stood for.

So much of the life of Senator David Croll was connected with the city of Windsor, and part of his provincial riding of Windsor- Walkerville is located within my Windsor West riding. Therefore you will understand why I want to rise and for a minute or two say something by way of tribute to the late Senator Croll.
He was always to the end of his days a strong voice for social justice, a strong voice for people in need, the elderly, the pensioners, the handicapped and the poor.
It is remarkable that he passed away after a full active day in his work as a senator, and I am sure he looked forward to being in our Liberal caucus this morning. He was always the first to arrive there. I must say it will not be the same coming to our caucus and not seeing Senator Croll already there to take part in the work of our caucus. When he took part in the work of our caucus he was always a progressive voice, a voice of reform and a voice of liberalism, both big and small /, in the best sense of the term.
I am sure his point of view, his attitudes, reflected his experience as an immigrant child who came with his family to Windsor from eastern Europe. I am sure his views, his attitudes, reflected very much the values of his Jewish heritage. I am sure they also reflected the concerns of the Windsor area, a city of hard working people from all over the world who came together in Windsor to build better lives for themselves and their families.
Dave Croll always worked for equality, fairness and reform. Mayor of Windsor at only 30 years of age, he helped his city to get through the devastation of the recession. His work in bringing together the former border cities created the city of Windsor as it is today.
His work as a member of the provincial legislature and as a member of the provincial cabinet did much to help the province get through the troubles and travails of the Great Depression of the thirties.
You will recall that as a member of the provincial legislature and as a cabinet minister, he helped establish in the province of Ontario basic programs of labour standards and social welfare which are the foundations of many of the programs of which we are so proud today.
Dave Croll always put the people first.
This was shown by what he said when he resigned from the Ontario cabinet because he did not agree with the views of his premier on the organization of workers in the trade unions. He said that he "would rather walk with the workers than ride with General Motors".
A recent biography of Dave Croll is entitled The People's Senator. Before he was the people's senator he was the people's member of Parliament from Toronto, the people's member of the legislature, the people's cabinet minister and the people's mayor of Windsor. Windsor has always been proud of Dave Croll and Windsor will always be proud of him. The city was, as I have said, so much a part of his life and his career.
June 12, 1991

I want to express my deepest sympathy to his family, his brother and his daughters. I want to say to this House that the greatest and strongest way we have of honouring the memory of Dave Croll is to ensure that the ideals for which he stood will continue to inspire all of us who seek to serve the public interest in this House and everywhere in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to state a few words because Senator Croll, when he was a member of this place, represented the riding of which I am now the representative. This man was a different kind of senator when one recalls that he spent his last day as an 11-hour day. That indicates the devotion that he had to this place. He was so much a symbol of Windsor. His imprint upon Windsor was exceedingly strong. It was strong among those who were poor. It was strong among those who worked for a living. It was exceedingly strong among those of us of many ethnic and racial groups in Windsor who looked for a voice of equality.
We will all miss him, but we will not lose what he gave us in Windsor and that is a character of generosity and care which he brought to this place as well.
I would like to express on behalf of my community and my party our condolences to the family and we share their sorrow in this loss.

speakeroldname: Hon. Lloyd Axworthy (Winnipeg South Centre) moved:
speechtext:
That this House affirm that Ministers are individually and collectively responsible to the House of Commons for the activities of government including the management and conduct of the Public Service; that, individually, Ministers are responsible for the administration of the decisions of the Government and the activities of Public Servants falling under their jurisdiction; and that, collectively, they are responsible for the decisions of the Government as a whole and the activities of their colleagues.
He said: Mr. Speaker, on May 8 press reports detailed how a former Iraqi ambassador to Washington by the name of Al-Mashat was given quick and accelerated access into Canada, apparently circumventing a number of the required procedures under the Immigration Act. It raised many questions about how preference and priority are afforded to special guests of the government.
Since that time the issue has become much bigger, much more serious, much more critical than the mere entry of Al-Mashat into Canada. In many ways it has gone to the very heart of accountability and responsibility of a parliamentary system of government. It has questioned the very credibility of several senior ministers of the present government. It has gone to the question of how trust and confidence, veracity and honesty have to be the currency of this House, and not a debased currency as is so often the case and as we have seen in the last three weeks.
Even today we saw the Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs complaining, perhaps whining, that this discussion and inquiry has hurt his own credibility; as if it was the responsibility of the opposition, as if it was the opposition that was responsible for ducking, bobbing, weaving, and evading its responsibility.
June 12, 1991

It was an attempt one more time to deflect the responsibility for a serious decision which no one had the guts, the courage, the sense of ethics, or parliamentary morality to stand up and take responsibility for.
I was recently reading a comment made by Malcolm Fraser, the Australian Prime Minister in 1982, which I thought would be good advice for members opposite to take. He said: "This government has always upheld the fundamental principle of ministerial responsibility" and "the appearance and reality of integrity are indispensable parts of our system of government". Integrity and responsibility are indispensable parts of our system of government, one that we share with the Australians.
In all the thousands of words that have been exchanged I have never yet once heard any member on the opposite side understand or admit that integrity and responsibility are an indispensable part of our system of government. If they had admitted it we would have had a very different story. We would have had a very different chronology of events. We would have had ministers standing up and saying: "Yes, Al-Mashat came in. I take responsibility for it. If you do not like it, what are you going to do about it?" In other words, defending the actions of the government.
Instead, we have had deflection, hiding, and evasion. Perhaps the most smarmy move of all was trying to take a couple of public servants and put them before the public saying: "They are the ones who caused the problem. It is their error in judgment, not ours".
Let us get down to facts. Let us deal with the specifics of the issue. First, let us deal with the former Secretary of State for External Affairs, the present minister of constitutional affairs who keeps saying: "I see no evil, hear no evil. I didn't know anything about it, had no responsibility. Don't touch me, I can't be held responsible for anything. After all it was only a decision made by my chief of staff, the person whom I appointed, the person I put into place, not a public servant, not some anonymous foreign service officer way off in Ankara or Vienna but the person who has offices right next to mine". Yet he said he had no responsibility. That is a
Supply
distortion of a fundamental principle of ministerial responsibility.
To compound the error, that minister, along with others, says: "It was the Associate Under-Secretary of State for External Affairs who did not inform me".
We even heard from the under-Secretary. It appears that in fact he was informed according to the procedures set out by the minister himself. It was not a matter of the Associate Under-Secretary forgetting. He did not say: "I am not going to tell the minister". He instructed a senior civil servant, the head of the Security Division of External Affairs, to write a memo detailing that Al-Mashat had been turned down as a defector and was now being considered as a possible retiree.
That memorandum went to the major departmental clerk of the minister's office who registered it. It came in an envelope marked secret, had a tab snapped on under red wax. It went from there to the office of a chief of staff who admits that he read it, but then he cannot recall what happened to it. All of a sudden he was struck with a fit of amnesia that has lasted for three months.
Actually, maybe the minister responsible is the minister of health and welfare. Maybe it is that he has not undertaken a major health inspection of all departmental assistants, all executive assistants, all chiefs of staffs and all ministers of the Crown who seem to have been struck by a mass epidemic of amnesia on the government side. All we heard in the testimony was: "I can't recall. I can't remember. I wasn't there. I don't know. I am not sure".
The fact of the matter is that the minister of constitutional affairs does bear full responsibility in terms of what goes on in his office.
I will take him at his word. He stood up in Parliament today and said: "I did not see it". We cannot dispute the word of a member.
At the same time it does beg a real question as to what happened to the memo. Does anybody in this entire country believe that a memo marked "Secret" sent under the proper procedures in the Department of External Affairs, which is probably the most self-conscious department in the entire country about security

June 12, 1991
Supply
matters, all of a sudden just vanishes overnight? It just sort of flutters away.
No such thing happened to it. That security memo is somewhere, but this government has made no effort to find it. It has not made any. I make this additional allegation, charge and submission to the government. If it is trying to defend the performance and activity of individual ministers, how is it possible to do so when there has been no real effort to call in the RCMP to properly investigate what happened to the memo or who is responsible for it?
When there was a small budget leak that a reporter from Global Television, Doug Small, received, half the legions of the RCMP were scouring the country looking for it.
When members of the opposition are sent a brown envelope and it arrives at their desk with some kind of government document within 24 hours the RCMP is in our office saying: "How did you get hold of that?"
The government goes to extraordinary lengths to change its typewritten cabinet documents and secret documents so it can trace them. However, all of a sudden in this one case there is a cavalier, casual approach.
The present minister of external affairs says: "I don't know. I have been away. I don't know". This is a minister who is operating in a total fit of absence and is not fulfilling her responsibility to find that document so that we can find out what is the truth.
I just heard the parliamentary secretary say: "We have it". Once again, another big lie. Once again, another piece of mythology. Once again, we are engaging in propaganda because that parliamentary secretary knows full well that the original had disappeared and he knows the original-

Certainly look at the "blues". What I was saying was that this government, day after day, attempts to manufacture new concoctions about what went on.
The parliamentary secretary is attempting to intimate that we have the document when he knows full well the original document has disappeared and that original document has stamped on it who received it and how it was used. If there is going to be any apology it should be from that parliamentary secretary who is directly responsible for shutting down the committee of inquiry by saying he refused to answer any questions.
Knowing that hon. member, I know we will not get an apology. I know when the apology will come. It will be the day when he has to face his electorate back in his own riding. It is going to demand the ultimate apology, which is the fact that will put him into permanent retirement.
Let us go on to the second case of ministerial responsibility. I want to cite very clearly the circumstances and the events that we know about.
Once it was discovered that Al-Mashat was in the country and it became public, the entire government geared into massive damage control.
We know that on May 13, there was a meeting held of senior cabinet ministers, including the minister of external affairs, the former Solicitor General, the Minister of Employment and Immigration, the minister for constitutional affairs, the Clerk of the Privy Council and the principal secretary to the Prime Minister. Did they get together to talk about, as we keep hearing, admonitions from the minister of external affairs to get down to the substance?
Did they get together to talk about what was happening in Kuwait or to the Kurdish refugees? No. They were planning on how they could issue a report that would be laundered and cleansed, and would carefully, selectively take the information which had been given to them by the pubic service auditors and refine it into a more acceptable document, missing key points, key facts, key elements and ingredients.
Those very same ministers had the unmitigated nerve and gall to come before the public on May 14 and say: "This is a complete document and it has all the facts,
June 12, 1991

everything you need to know. Nothing more needs to be said".
The very day before this high level committee of ministers and senior officials had spent its time whiting out the important parts, twisting the words, rewriting and regauging. To compound the problem once again, it engaged in what I can only call an act of political extortion. The committee wrote into that report apologies or confessions for Mr. Raymond Chretien, the Associate Under-Secretary and for Mr. Daubney, even though neither of those two gentlemen had ever been asked if they were prepared to apologize. They had never been given the opportunity to give their side of the case to that committee. This committee was a star chamber, a kangaroo court. It is running people out on a rail.
Once it was revealed, once that information came to light and we knew that a senior group of ministers and officials had engaged in this kind of political concoction, not one of them had the guts or the courage to stand in the House and apologize to the individuals involved for ruining their reputations. In fact those ministers and officials gloated over it.
The minister of external affairs in a press conference said: "Of course this is going to undermine their reputation". There are several people whose reputations have been undermined. It is not the Associate Under-Secretary. It is the minister of external affairs, the minister for constitutional affairs and the Minister of Employment and Immigration. That is really where the crux of this whole issue lies.
One does not have to take my word for it.
Let me just read, if I may for a few moments, the comments of other people who have had some serious and distinguished experience in government. Mr. A1 Johnson, who was a former deputy minister, in a May 23 article in The Citizen, said: "The pick and choose approach to ministerial responsibility is lunacy. Ministers would be free to choose what they would accept responsibility for; everything that went well, of course, they would agree with; anything that went wrong it was the civil servants to blame".
Let me also cite the judgment of Judge Lieff in the Goyer case in 1978: "It is a long-standing convention of parliamentary democracy and the doctrine of ministerial responsibility which encompasses it that civil servants are to remain faceless to the public. A minister should not be
Supply
able to blame or castigate personally any civil servant or department under his control".
We then come to a third authority, and this is an authority I hope the government will listen to because it was the authority cited ad nauseam by the minister of external affairs. Professor Kenneth Kemaghan, on the whole concept of ministerial responsibility, said: "In the event of maladministration by department officials, the conventions of both ministerial responsibility and political neutrality require that ministers protect the anonymity of the wrongdoers by declining to identify them publicly".
He goes on to explain that also the burden of proof is on the ministers to be responsible.
Let me also quote once again from J. R. Mallory who was the authority cited by the minister of external affairs as taking away her obligation to be accountable: "A minister alone is accountable for the policy of his department; the civil servant cannot be called to account for policy statements or his actions". That was J. R. Mallory, one of the distinguished political scientists.
The reason why it is important that this House face this issue and come to grips with it, and why members of both sides of the House must support this motion is in recognition of the damage that has been done. Until we reassert this fundamental principle of responsibility there is going to be a continued undermining of the confidence of the Public Service of this country. Officials in external affairs will never again be able to trust their minister after she railroaded one of their senior officials into the kind of public ignominy that she was responsible for.
All public servants across Canada are right now saying to themselves: "I am not taking the responsibility. I am not making the decision because I am going to be hung out to dry by those ministers".
That is one reason why this House must reaffirm this principle. We must also reaffirm confidence in the way that this government works because we see time and time again ministers evading the truth, not detailing the facts, blaming other people, and fingering public servants. We are all talking about this scepticism. The throne speech said in such eloquent words that we must restore belief in the parliamentary system. I can think of no more serious erosion to the parliamentary system

Supply
than what has been constituted by these ministers not taking responsibility and accountability for their actions. That is where the real responsibility lies. That is when confidence is undermined; when ministers get up in this House and play deaf and dumb to their own responsibilities. That is not the way to conduct oneself.
Over the years this government has been on a wrecking crusade. It has undermined the CBC. It has undermined our public transportation system. It undermined the economy of this country and people are paying a heavy price for it. Now, not satisfied with ripping apart the economic and social fabric of Canada, it is trying to undermine the Parliament of Canada and the very system which we are all sworn to defend and protect.
Until we can reaffirm what is important to it and until we can say to Canadians very clearly that we are going to try to rebuild that system and show ministers who are elected to take accountability, that the buck stops at their desk and not at somebody else's desk, there will not be confidence in this system of government and there will not be confidence that people can be governed with honesty, truth and veracity.
The government shut down the parliamentary inquiry probably because we are getting too close to the truth. It can redeem itself by having a judicial inquiry where it is not subject to parliamentary majorities, so that there can be oaths of office, so that there can be proper investigation, so that we can get a kind of real insight.
If the government is not prepared to do that there is another way. I would like to cite the comments of Lord Carrington, a distinguished British minister and former Secretary of State for External Affairs.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, seriously, this is a very important fundamental principle we are discussing, the principle of ministerial responsibility. It underlines our system of responsible government.
Recent events of which we in this House are all aware have given rise to considerable comment from members of Parliament, the public, the press, about the nature and practice of this principle. Indeed, the motion which we are debating shows that interest in this principle is alive and well in this Parliament, as it should be. I would note, however, that some of the comments on ministerial responsibility which we have heard and read in recent weeks have contained some misconceptions about the principle that have undoubtedly confused rather than clarified how it is applied in Canada.
I am pleased, therefore, to participate today in this debate and set out for the House, and through it for the Canadian public, the key elements of this fundamental principle of our democratic system of government.
I wish first to address the motion itself. On the face of it, it is a very straightforward motion calling upon members of Parliament to announce their support for the doctrine of ministerial responsibility. The vehicle being used, as has been conceded by the Liberal Party opposite in another supply motion earlier this year, the medicare one, is a non-confidence motion. Were it to pass, it would require the government to resign. We can hardly expect this as a straightforward attempt on the part of the Liberal Party to encourage non-partisan all-party support for the principles underlying this doctrine to which this government has adhered faithfully in recent events.
Let me therefore set out for the House the nature and elements of this doctrine.
Ministers exercise powers bestowed upon them by the Crown in Parliament and hold office at the pleasure of the Crown. The exercise of these powers for which ministers are constitutionally responsible to Parliament provides the foundation of responsible government.
The concentration of responsibility in the hands of ministers reflects the fundamental democratic principle that the power of the state must be exercised under the authority of elected officials accountable to the representatives of the electorate.
This enables Parliament to focus responsibility for the conduct of government on those of its members who hold ministerial office and who ultimately must personally answer to Parliament and hence to the electorate for their actions and the actions of their subordinates. Collectively ministers are responsible for the decisions of the government as a whole and the activities of all of their colleagues, even though Mr. Trudeau did not agree with that. This is the cement of our system of government. Although collective responsibility unlike individual responsibility is conventional rather than legal, it is fashioned through means that serve to make more effective the exercise of individual responsibility.
In this manner the constitutional responsibility of ministers, both individually and collectively, enables Parliament to satisfy itself that power is exercised responsibly through the system of government.
June 12, 1991

The direct responsibility of ministers to Parliament on a day-to-day basis is the essential strength of our system. The essence of the doctrine is that ministers, and only ministers, answer to the House for the way in which the authority conferred on them has been exercised.
The principles of responsibility, the concentration of the Crown's power in the hands of ministers and the subjection of ministerial power to parliamentary control reinforce the responsibility of ministers, requiring them to be in a position to assure the House that they are exercising powers responsibly.
Ministers fulfil their responsibilities and are called to account by the House of Commons for the exercise of their statutory authority in accordance with practice and convention. From the origins of our system, however, political circumstances rather than literal application of the principle of ministerial responsibility have governed the answerability of ministers. As Professor J. R. Mallory has noted, the minister has a political responsibility.
Ministers are responsible for all the actions taken under their authority. Although it is true that the degree to which they are required to answer for the actions of officials will depend upon the political circumstances and whether an official has, for example, acted in a clearly unacceptable manner of which the minister had no knowledge, the fact remains that the minister is constitutionally responsible. This is essential in determining who answers for what and to whom in the system.
Accountability in the system derives directly from the responsibility of ministers. Ministers answer before Parliament and are challenged to defend the way in which they or their officials have exercised the power that is made legitimate my their constitutional responsibility as ministers.

programs carried out under the statutory authority exercised by ministers. They are loyal to their ministers and are required to actively support and participate in the policy and administrative decisions taken by ministers individually and collectively. Put simply, deputy ministers are responsible to ministers.
Officials are not, of course, constitutionally responsible, but they play and have played a role vis-a-vis Parliament that in some important respects compliments the role of ministers. Although officials do not have constitutional responsibility or share the responsibility of their ministers, they do share to a degree in the answerability of their ministers to Parliament.
They support ministers in answering to committees of the House provided this does not draw officials into partisan controversy or undermine the authority and responsibility of ministers. This role of officials has been enhanced and strengthened by the McGrath report which recommended that public servants be made available to parliamentary committees. The government stated at that time that it supported this recommendation, and recent events have borne out our commitment in this regard.
The concentration of responsibility in the hands of ministers is the bedrock of parliamentary government. It is, however, a matter of observation that the government is a large administrative enterprise. It is not a modem phenomenon that ministers cannot know everything that is under their authority. The phenomenon is merely more acute today than it was a century ago, and not prima facie proof of the irrelevance of ministerial responsibility. Ministers spend much of their time providing information to Parliament, indicating a need for the minister's ability to answer and provide information to be shared without, however, sharing his or her responsibility.
The essential elements of the doctrine of ministerial responsibility, therefore, are that: Power flows from the Crown and is exercised by ministers who are responsible to Parliament. Ministers are responsible for the actions of their officials, whether they had prior knowledge of them or not. Officials advise ministers and they are accountable to ministers.

When an error is made of which the minister is unaware, the minister acts to establish the facts, correct the error and satisfy himself or herself that it will not reoccur. The minister informs the House of the action taken.
I note that all the precedents at the federal level in Canada and Canadian authorities support this interpretation of the doctrine.
Professor Kenneth Kernaghan has noted it is almost universally accepted that it is unreasonable to hold a minister personally responsible in the form of resignation for the administrative failings of subordinates.
The usual practice is that the minister informs Parliament that the fault lies with his officials, and he promises that the offenders will be disciplined and their mistakes corrected.

When we speak of minister's individual responsibility we merely mean that, for every act or neglect on the part of civil servants, some minister or other is charged to explain in the Houses of Parliament: and that only ministers may do so.

In June 1976 a Liberal cabinet minister, Jean-Pierre Goyer, had blamed a senior bureaucrat for a bungled deal to buy military aircraft. He was a fellow named Stopforth and was one of his senior bureaucrats.
The minister stood up and said: "No, no, it was not my responsibility. It was the senior bureaucrat's responsibility". What was the response at that time by members of the Conservative Party who were then in opposition, including the member for Surrey-White Rock-South Langley? What did he have to say about it at that time? I have the Hansard here that the member referred to earlier.
What did the member for Yellowhead, who was then the Leader of the Opposition say about this attempt to pass the buck to civil servants? He said that his question arose out of the attempt by the minister to transfer blame for this government's gross incompetence in the Lockheed affair to a middle ranking civil servant. He said

it was shameful to try to pass that blame to a middle ranking civil servant.
The Conservative defence critic, Allan McKinnon, accused the minister of "trying to blame his own incompetence and lack of supervision on his subordinates".
It is interesting that when it is in opposition the Conservative Party is prepared to stand and defend public servants. When it is in government, what does it do? It engages in the sleaziest form of buck passing in an attempt to avoid its own responsibility in allowing Mo-hamed Al-Mashat to enter the country.
There is a double standard, and I think Canadians recognize veiy clearly that double standard.
I want to take a couple of minutes first of all to just put this question in context. The member for Winnipeg South Centre certainly did that in the course of his comments with respect to what took place before Al-Mashat got into the country, but also with respect to what took place afterward.
I think many Canadians are asking themselves two fundamental questions. How did the guy get into the country in the first place without any minister knowing? Second, what is this absurd, dangerous and destructive spectacle that we have seen in this country of ministers trying to cover up their own responsibility, trying to doctor documents, seeing documents disappearing and extorting confessions from public servants? There are two issues here. There is the original question of how this guy got into the country, but there is also the very fundamental question that members on the Conservative side of this House are refusing to allow the committee to deal with, the question of ministerial accountability.
Certainly the motion which is before the House merely reaffirms a principle which the Secretary of State for External Affairs set out as representing the policy of the Government of Canada in an appearance before the committee on May 30. In fact it quotes from that statement verbatim.
How is it that members of the Conservative Party now are going to vote against that statement which purports to represent the policy of this government? We are told
by the government House leader that somehow the government will fall if they support this statement. The government members, including the government House leader in 1986, supported the McGrath report. What did the McGrath report have to say about questions of confidence on supply days?
It said that confidence on supply days was a question for the government to consider and that the motion is only a question of confidence if the government declares it to be a question of confidence. This nonsense that somehow the government is going to collapse, is going to fall if it reaffirms this principle of ministerial accountability, should not be accepted by this House.
At the conclusion of my remarks I will move an amendment to this motion that will make it very clear that by supporting the motion before the House, members of the House are not in any way considering a lack of confidence in the government. Not by supporting this motion alone. Certainly there are many other reasons for voting lack of confidence in this government, but it will not be able to say that voting for this motion represents that.
I want to look at the question of ministerial accountability. I want to look at the role that ministers have played in this process. Before doing that, I think it is also important to put this question in the context of what has happened here and the anger that Canadians feel and have felt since May 7 or 8, when they first learned that something had gone very wrong, that Mohammed Al-Mashat, the former Iraqi Ambassador to the United States, had not only been allowed to immigrate to Canada but had been given the royal treatment, the red carpet treatment.
We know that he had friends in high places. Apparently Allan Gotlieb and John Godfrey, and who knows who else, made representations to senior government officials urging that Al-Mashat be allowed into the country. We know only too well of the record of Al-Mashat. We know, for example, that when he was Ambassador of Iraq in the United Kingdom he actively encouraged a young reporter for The London Observer, Farzard Bazoft, to make visits to Iraq. After Mr. Bazoft had been arrested in Iraq and falsely charged with espionage, and many countries around the world including Canada con-

demned that, we know that Al-Mashat denounced him as a spy. He found the secret trial and the hanging of Bazoft thoroughly justifiable.
We know that this man was an important member of the ruling Ba'ath party. We know that he justified the holding of what he called "guests", hostages, including innocent Canadians during the period leading up to the war. We know of this man's record. We have to ask ourselves why it was that, despite this record, this man was given the red carpet treatment. What deals were made, for example, between the American State Department, American intelligence agencies and Canada, to allow this man to get the royal treatment, this special treatment?
This is particularly offensive to Canadians who, in many cases, have struggled with the bureaucracy of the department of immigration themselves for two, three or four years, seeking to be reunited with their families, with their loved ones. When they see this kind of thing happening, they are angry and they ask who is responsible and they see ministers running for cover.
Refugees who have waited in this country for fair treatment have, in some cases, out of desperation, committed suicide. Others ask themselves: why is Al-Mashat getting special treatment, when at the same time there is a system in which refugees are being denied justice. They know. They have seen the desperate Kurds fleeing from injustice and they ask themselves why there is one standard for Al-Mashat and another for the Kurds.
I might add that Al-Mashat, speaking of the Kurds, also denied that there had been any chemical warfare or any gassing whatsoever of the Kurds at Halabja in 1988, despite the fact that the eyes of the world saw exactly what was going on.
Why is it that this man is given the red carpet treatment? On May 8 the Minister of Employment and Immigration threw up his hands and said: "Nobody knew, Mr. Speaker. I just found out. We all just found out and what a terrible thing it is". I do not think Canadians accept that.
We have slowly been learning that in fact ministers did know earlier. We learned, for example, that the Solicitor General found out on April 11. We learned that the Minister of Employment and Immigration found out on April 16. What did she do when she found out? She said

Did this minister do that? Did she follow her own guidelines? No, she did not do a damn thing when she found out on April 16. She did not tell the new minister, her successor, Mr. Valcourt: "Bernard, something went wrong here, get to the bottom of it and find out". After all, she and Mr. Clark had earlier turned down another application by another Iraqi diplomat. She did not get on the phone to him or talk to him and say: "Something has gone wrong here". We are told that the Prime Minister only found out on April 30. The Clerk of the Privy Council knew that he had already jumped to the front of the queue. He had had his interviews, his medical and his interviews for a security check and everything had been done. It was a done deal.
Immigration knew and CSIS knew and yet we are asked to believe that nobody told any minister. That is what we are asked to believe. The fact is that, even after Al-Mashat got into the country and the Privy Council Office was informed on April 2 that the guy was in the country, it took 29 days. What did they do then? According to the Privy Council Office they did nothing. The Clerk of the Privy Council did not even tell the Prime Minister until April 30, four weeks after he found out.
The legislative assistant to the Prime Minister knew. The deputy press secretary to the Prime Minister knew. The Solicitor General knew. The Minister of Employment and Immigration knew. We are told the Prime Minister did not find out until April 30. The Secretary of State for External Affairs, the new Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs, did not find out until May 7. Incredible, literally incredible.

June 12, 1991
Supply
We raise concerns about a meeting that took place of ministers, a cabinet lynch mob, that was deciding to extort confessions from senior public servants. They decided for the sake of symmetry that they would name the minister's chief of staff. It was a cabinet meeting that decided that they would deliberately issue a misleading and inaccurate document, an inaccurate chronology of events. What does the Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs say when we tiy to raise questions about this? He says: "Don't touch me. Don't ask questions about my credibility because you might damage my credibility as Captain Canada". Unbelievable. That is what this minister says to Canadians: "Do not ask me tough questions. Do not put me on the spot because it might hurt my credibility".
His credibility and the credibility of his fellow ministers have already been damaged by their own incompetence in dealing with this affair.
What about the events that led up to the entry of Al-Mashat into the country? We know that a number of senior officials were well aware of the fact that he would be allowed into the country, fast-tracked. We know that there was a memo on May 7 that set out clearly that Al-Mashat had already been accepted provisionally as a retired applicant. He had had his medicals. Yet despite that immigration officials did not alert their minister. Privy Council Office officials did not alert their minister, the Prime Minister. The officials responsible for CSIS did not alert the Solicitor General.
The one public official who made an effort to alert his minister was the one public official that this government has attempted to blame. Shameful. The one public servant who not only followed the guidelines then in place, and it is ministers who are responsible for those guidelines, the one public servant who followed those guidelines is hung out to dry by these ministers.
Why did they do nothing whatsoever to finger Arthur Kroeger, the deputy minister of immigration, who admitted before the committee that he should have said something too but did nothing? Why did they not finger Paul Tellier who said: "Yes, I knew, but I did not tell the Prime Minister until April 30". It is pretty obvious why they only fingered one public servant.
Of course they also fingered David Daubney for symmetry. Why did they tell Daubney they were fingering him? Because of the fact that Raymond Chretien happened to be the nephew of the Leader of the Opposition and they thought that would not look very good.
Mr. Speaker, you are certainly right. Canadians find that this whole matter does not look very good because they know that it is an attempt to evade and avoid the responsibility of cabinet ministers by blaming one public servant who, in fact, did follow the existing procedures.
In my mind it is not unreasonable to suggest in all the circumstances that given the seriousness of Al-Mashat's potential entry to the country Raymond Chretien could have taken additional steps to ensure that this matter came to the attention of the minister responsible. I do not dispute that fact. I do not dispute the fact that apparently he agreed to have a memo sent by Mr. Vincent, but as I understand it there was no follow-up. There were a number of meetings between himself and the deputy minister, a number of meetings with the minister, and I do not disagree that it is not unreasonable to suggest that given the gravity of the situation identified by Mr. Chretien himself that perhaps he could have taken additional steps to ensure that the minister knew.
But to single him out as the only person responsible and to issue a statement stating that Mr. Chretien had apologized knowing full well that that statement was a lie, a bald-faced lie, is what Canadians find reprehensible.
In the time remaining available to me I want to remind members of this House what the now Secretary of State for External Affairs said during the press conference when she decided to pin the blame on Raymond Chretien. She said: "I don't think anyone should underestimate the impact this could have on people's reputations. You know the saying about taking away my good name".
I think Canadians are going to judge this government and judge it very harshly both in terms of Mohamed Al-Mashat coming into this country, getting the red carpet treatment, and also in terms of the shameful way that ministers of the Crown have attempted to avoid their own responsibility and to pin that on others.
June 12, 1991

By trying to blame public servants they have very seriously damaged the relationship between the Public Service and the government, and the Canadian people are going to call them to account for that responsibility.

speakeroldname: Mr. Benno Friesen (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not go out of my way to agree with the hon. member very often, but there is one point that he did raise which I agree with. It is frequently the case when members of government, for example, will take positions they may have attacked while they were in opposition. Certainly members of the opposition will attack positions they were defending when they were in the government. That is true not only for the Liberals and the Tories. It is also true for the New Democrats. They are really no different.
I read where Premier Bob Rae, in the Ontario legislature said: "The opposition talks about ministerial responsibility. I have looked into the precedents and there is not a case that I can find in the last 50 years where a minister was expected to take the rap, the fall, because something was done without him knowing about it".
There seems to be a doctrine for Premier Rae and the Ontario legislature and another one for the New Democrats here in Ottawa. Why is it that Rae takes one position and Robinson takes another? It seems to me that if he wants to criticize people for taking opposing positions, depending on whether they are government or opposition, he should include the New Democrats. They are really caught in the same human web that we are.
He says that Canadians are angry that Al-Mashat came in too rapidly. You bet your boots they are angry. So is the government. So are members of the government. Every one of us here has cases in our files that we think have been there far too long and that we would like to see come in. We have constituents who want to see their relatives and friends come in, and they have not been able to. They are offended, as we are offended. Please, please, it is foolhardy for the member to go into high dudgeon, thinking that only the opposition and other people are offended. We are just as offended as they are and we want that to stop.
He began his statement by talking about the strong-arm tactics bringing the committee to an end.
Supply
He is right.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
We can count on the member for Hamilton East to echo that. She never fails us.
He is criticizing the committee for stopping and yet on June 7, almost a week ago, he said on CBC: "I do not think we have to prolong this thing indefinitely. Some Conservative members of the committee had suggested that we hear from Allan Gotlieb, but I think Canadians expect us to report and to report soon on what went wrong on this and how Al-Mashat got into the country".
He cannot have it both ways. I do have a question for him. He is offended by the fast-tracking of Mr. Al-Mashat, but I remember when he was first elected back in the dim ages of history, before the House sat. He encountered a Latin American seaman who had jumped ship in Vancouver. He had been in several countries after he left Latin America and jumped ship in Vancouver and the member for Burnaby-Kingsway all of a sudden on his own decided: "Here is a refugee". He took him to his apartment and sheltered this man and badgered the then minister of immigration to make sure this fellow whom he harboured was going to be declared a refugee.
Here today he is offended that Mr. Al-Mashat got a fast-track, and all the time in his own history he has been trying to fast-track people himself. Tell me, where is this guy coming from?

Mr. Speaker, I will be very pleased to respond to the questions of the hon. member.
With respect to Galindo Madrid, a young Chilean refugee who had been a student leader and had been tortured in Chile, perhaps the member recalls that Amnesty International, the United Nations Human Rights Commission and the United Nations Commission on Refugees said this was an outrage and that his life was in danger. The Conservative government however, which he was a part of, was prepared to send this person back to be tortured and possibly to be killed.
I and the many others such as church leaders from across this country, including Mennonite church leaders and perhaps the hon. member might have listened to them at the time, stood up and said: "We will not stand by while a Chilean refugee is sent back to a bloodthirsty and brutal military dictatorship to be tortured and killed".

Maybe the hon. member could explain why the Prime Minister stood up in this House on May 15 and said that the Clerk of the Privy Council had said: "Do not let Al-Mashat in. Do not admit him".

Mr. Speaker, I want to make a comment on the matters presented by the member for Burnaby.
I want to make it clear to him and to members of the House that when he refers to the dialogue between the Prime Minister of Canada and the Clerk of the Privy Council, Mr. Paul Tellier, Mr. Tellier said to the committee, and the member heard it, that what the Prime Minister said was 100 per cent accurate.
Read it. It is there in writing and it is in the public domain.

It is ironic that in this case the member for Burnaby and the member for Winnipeg South Centre went to Baghdad. They said: "We have to deal with the Iraqis. We have to bring about peace. We have to negotiate. We have to talk".
The minute a former member of the administration in Iraq, the Ambassador to the United States, comes into Canada, they said: "That should not happen". I would have thought they would welcome him to Canada.
It was this side which decided to take action against Iraq. It was the government that entered into hostilities and it was the members opposite in the NDP who said: "No, no hostilities". The Leader of the Opposition said: "Bring our men home".
My question is on another subject. I want to refer to what occurred in the committee, and the member knows this. Mr. Anthony Vincent gave a statement to the committee explaining exactly what he had done and he asked to share with Mr. Raymond Chretien any blame that should be attached.

"While I greatly appreciate Mr. Chretien's readiness to shoulder the entire burden of public responsibility on behalf of the department, I consider it only just that the public be aware of my own role in the recent events".

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to make a very long presentation. It has been extremely well documented by the two previous speakers from this side what happened in the Al-Mashat affair.
For me, of course, it is unbelievable, and I know there are a lot of Canadians who cannot believe the story given by the government. We know there were apparently some problems in the Department of External Affairs, but there were three departments involved in that. We have now found, in the committee, that there were bureaucrats in every department who had been aware of the Al-Mashat application for a long time. There were all sorts of communications between departments and so on.
In one case there was a bureaucrat by the name of McCallion working in the office of the then minister of external affairs who was going on holidays and who was involved in security matters. Anybody who has been minister of external affairs or who has been a minister in any department, will know how serious the Department of External Affairs takes anything that involves security. It is for them an extremely important domain and they take it extremely seriously. Before she went on holidays she said to Mr. Daubney, who is the No.l bureaucrat in the office of the minister: "Be aware it is a very dangerous problem and it is extremely urgent. I am going away, but make sure that the minister is informed".
However, to make sure that it would work properly, she decided on her own, according to her own testimony, to talk to other people in the office of the minister to make sure that the minister was aware.
It must have been the same story in every other department, but we do not know. What we know is that
Supply
nobody from the other departments has been blamed for anything. We are all very surprised that the Solicitor General's department, again specializing in security matters, would not inform its minister. These are things that we cannot believe. There are dozens of people in the bureaucracy who must have known and suddenly we see that some junior people in the offices of the ministers make other departments aware of what is going on and it never goes to the top.
I have been a minister for 17 years myself and I know one thing that is very basic. The main document, signed by the official when it is decided it has to go to the minister, is the copy that eventually will be on the desk of the minister. It is the proper thing to do. We never gave a copy to the minister. We gave him the original document signed by the bureaucrats. This is the procedure.
The original is there and did not go anywhere but to Mr. Daubney. According to the rules decided by external affairs it went there, but the original document does not exist any more. It is, as it was raised in the House today, a question of security. For a much smaller thing, the whole government is getting very excited about security.
Do you remember what happened when there was a leak with the budget? We have never seen so many policemen involved in something on the Hill. Members who received brown envelopes were asked by the RCMP where they came from. Now we have a document that is at the heart of a major controversy and it has disappeared. Nobody knows where it is.
It is very strange.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
It is very, very strange.

I find this hard to believe. When I was a kid, people would say it was a mystery. What is a mystery? It is something you cannot understand but you have to believe it because it was revealed by God.
In this case, the revealing was done by the Prime Minister or by the former Secretary of State for External Affairs. Some mystery. Everybody in the department knew. As one member said not long ago, even the minister's chauffeur knew. Everybody in three departments knew about it, except the ministers.

June 12, 1991
Supply
One wonders, however, and this has not been addressed in the House, why the three ministers involved in the Al-Mashat affair were transferred all of a sudden. Why? According to parliamentary practice, the minister of a department is obliged to field questions on that department in the House. Meanwhile there were some changes in cabinet. The former minister for external affairs who is now Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs can no longer field questions about internal matters related to the Department of External Affairs. The minister who was responsible for immigration was transferred to external affairs so she can no longer answer on behalf of the Department of Employment and Immigration. Then, all of sudden, our Solicitor General who was doing a pretty good job disappeared. He got a nice promotion, but I am not sure to what department.
What happened? It is a mystery. We have to believe it even if we do not understand. It sounds slightly ridiculous. Personally I see an aspect that is even more troubling; We can debate whether Al-Mashat should or should not have been admitted to Canada, but it is obvious that at some time there was a conspiracy. How can we get out of this mess? On May 13, the day before the new Minister of Employment and Immigration, and the new minister for external affairs made their statements, there was a meeting. I think this is the most serious element, because the meeting included ministers and bureaucrats.

There were ministers there and there were bureaucrats and they decided at that moment: "How can we get out of this?" They had a report that had been prepared by very responsible officials. When they saw that report they gave instructions to change it. After they decided that they asked how they could get out of it. Suddenly they gave instructions to extract apologies. It was unbelievable that the chief of staff for the minister of external affairs, a former member of Parliament, was suddenly informed-he said nobody had asked him any questions, not one single question-that he had to apologize and that he would have to take the blame.
For symmetry.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
For symmetry. After that they singled out a bureaucrat who had to take the blame. They told
him to apologize and take the blame. Who did that? They were the ministers of the Crown of this country who gathered in the cabinet room to determine who were guilty and who were to be informed of their guilt without having a chance to explain themselves.
Shame.
A kangaroo court.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
That was the day when they decided to hang two honourable people out there. Suppose that Mr. Daubney who served in this House would like to run again. He cannot because he had to play dumb in order to save his government. You know they killed him. That is what happened.
I was a cabinet minister for 17 years and I took my share of flak. I have a lot of scars, but never, never in my life would I have dared to blame someone for something for which I was responsible.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
When you are a minister and your bureaucrats do well, you take the credit. I always took the credit. I never got up in this House and said: "Do not thank me for that; say thank you to this bureaucrat". Never. I said: "Thank you very much". I took all the credit. On the other side of the ledger, when I made a mistake I took the blame. I never ran away from it. It is the only way.
Today I was coming back from Atlantic Canada when I met a young bureaucrat from the Quebec government at the airport. He was travelling to Ottawa. We were waiting because the plane was delayed, and we sat together. I asked him about that. He said to me: "I do not know if I can still do the job I am doing; I am paid to make decisions on a daily basis". He gave me some examples and I understood the political difficulty of some of the problems he has to deal with. He said to me: "I do not know if I would still be able to do that, because I do not know if my minister one day would get up in the House in Quebec and say, I blame him, I am not responsible". He said he had been a bureaucrat for 20 years and had always presumed that when he was working in his department he had a minister who would come to his defence if he made a mistake. He would be
June 12, 1991

reprimanded. He might have been demoted. He might have been changed, but nobody would have known that.
Now we have exactly the reverse situation. We have two people who have been blamed by this government, but they keep their jobs. They say it is just a little slap, take the blame. Normally if they have done something they should not have done, no one would know. One was appointed by the minister himself, the chief of staff. It was a job that was created by this government and in many ways it was a slap in the face for the bureaucracy. Government members felt that they needed a very senior person in every department who was not a bureaucrat, and everything had to go through that person.
For 17 years I was a minister in eight different departments. I did not need anyone between me and my deputy minister. I knew they were there to serve me to the best of their abilities. I knew that if they did well I would do well. And if I did well then they would do well too. I was to claim the fame if they did well, and I would have to take the blame if there was an error.
Today we have a certain number of ministers who met and we do not even know who was there. We do not know who was there.
They will not tell us.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
A certain number of bureaucrats were gathered together but we do not know what happened. We had a committee for a few days. No one was sworn in. Sometimes in front of the committee when it was a very delicate situation, bureaucrats or others were invited to be sworn in to give them freedom. In that case there was no such thing. And they are closing down that committee as quickly as they can.
There were a certain number of ministers there. I do not know who they were. I have an idea. They are the ones today who are in very responsible jobs, who will be dealing with their bureaucrats, who will be asking these people to make decisions, who will be asking these people to use their best judgment.
How can they face them and say: "I have confidence in you" or ask them: "Have you got confidence in your minister?" This is the question, because confidence and trust are the key of public office. The example given by
Supply
the member for Winnipeg South Centre earlier concerning Lord Carrington is a good example of what is noble in public life.
He said: "There is a mess. Somebody has to take the blame. I am at the top and I take the blame". He did not try to find anybody. He did not say he was not informed. He did not say he was not wakened in the middle of the night or whatever it was. He said: "I am responsible. I will do the honourable thing. I will get out".
Pass the buck.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
He did not pass the buck; it stopped with him.
The only thing I am asking these ministers is now that we are in a very difficult period of our history, can they really handle the job they have. After a mess like this one when the principal secretary to the Prime Minister, the secretary to the cabinet, the deputy ministers and the ministers gathered together and selected two bureaucrats to blame, they did not even ask them what they had done. How can the people of Canada trust these ministers today?
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
When we opened this session the government came to us and said: "Let's work together; this country is facing a major problem", and we offered our collaboration because we felt it was our duty. But to be faced with a government that acts like this, the rule is very simple. You take the blame when something is wrong and you do not finger anybody else but yourself. This is what a person of dignity does.
That is why I did not get into this debate, did not ask one question. I have been around since 1963 and I know there is a principle. It is responsibility.
The minute you become a cabinet minister, you take responsibility and you discharge responsibility until the end. That is the rule that should prevail. That is the one rule that can keep the confidence of the people in any individual.
In my judgment, the standards of integrity and trust were breached on May 13 when senior bureaucrats and senior ministers gathered together, including ministers who have nothing to do with the file any more, to protect themselves, wrap themselves in the flag or whatever it is rather than face the responsibility.

That is why I am voting with my party on this motion. It goes to the heart of responsible government. If that principle is broken, if the people who are elected to serve the country cannot take full responsibility, cannot defend the personal staff they selected to do the job, cannot fire them after they have said they have made a mistake, but instead single out somebody in the bureaucracy is wrong. Of all the departments, only the Department of External Affairs took the step to make sure that the minister knew.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
To single out a bureaucrat in that department who has done his job, plus the people working for him who have done their jobs, is unbelievable. Not one person in Immigration was singled out and it was an Immigration case. Not one single person in Immigration has been singled out.
It is a case of high security and nobody in the Solicitor General's department or CSIS has been singled out. It is not acceptable that they sweep it under the rug. They can do it; they have the majority. We will vote against it.
However, I would like to tell the people of Canada that when we form the government, every minister in the cabinet that I will be presiding over will have to take full responsibility for what is going on in his department. If there is any bungling in the department, nobody will be singled out. The minister will have to take the responsibility. If there are errors, some people might be moved, but people who cannot defend themselves will not be singled out, and left hanging out there in front of the public. It is shameful. It is an indignity that we have not seen in Canada for a long time and it is why I stood today.
If the system of ministerial responsibility and integrity is not respected, if ministers cannot go home and look at themselves in the mirror and say: "Do I have the trust of my employees, do I have the trust of the people of Canada," if they cannot do that because they want to keep their little jobs, people will never have confidence in public servants in Canada.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, I want to preface my question to the hon. Leader of the Opposition by congratulating him on a very eloquent speech in which he set out very well the fundamental principles of cabinet accountability, which I am sure that Prime Minister Audrey McLaughlin will implement when she forms the government after the next federal election.
The Leader of the Opposition has had 17 years, I believe, of experience as a minister. I wonder if he could comment on two particular aspects. First of all, the hon. Leader of the Opposition raised the issue of David Daubney and the way in which he was singled out in terms of symmetry. I think, in fairness, it has to be pointed out that Mr. Daubney was after all the chief of staff of the minister responsible at the time, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, that he stated that he did not know who Al-Mashat was, that he had no idea, that it could be any one of a whole series of former Iraqi ambassadors to the United States. He said that the memo was not highlighted. He did not bring it to the minister's attention.
While I agree that he was singled out for unfair treatment, I think that the Leader of the Opposition would agree that in the circumstances he did not do his job, but it was the minister who should be responsible for that, presumably. It was the minister who hired him. It was the minister presumably. In fact I think it is the Prime Minister who appoints chiefs of staff. It is the Prime Minister in consultation with the Secretary of State for External Affairs who has kept this person in place.
I wonder if the Leader of the Opposition could comment with respect to that aspect of accountability, and particularly the accountability of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, now Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs, for his own senior public servant.
Second and just briefly, perhaps the hon. Leader of the Opposition could comment on the defence that we heard earlier today in this House from the Minister responsible for the Constitution who said: "Don't attack me. You know it is not fair that you attack me because I am the minister responsible for the future of the country. I am the minister responsible for the Constitution". How does the Leader of the Opposition respond
June 12, 1991

to the suggestion that somehow we should lay off questioning this minister because of his present constitutional responsibilities?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
On the question of Mr. Daubney, I feel sorry for that gentleman. He has been put in an impossible position. He has failed to serve his minister so much that he should have been fired. There is something fishy there as to why he has not been fired.
It is probably because he decided to take the blame as he was asked. It was quite evident. "We need two scapegoats and you are one of them. But the price is, take the flak and we will keep you in your job". I think that it is a terrible position, that he did not even have the chance to talk to the people who were doing the inquiry.
He is the one person who admitted that he was not given the document and he does not know where the original is. He is the one who gets the originals of all documents on his desk and he does not know where it is. But he took the flak and he has not been fired. He is still doing that.
You cannot blame him. You can only blame the person who named him. Not him. I do not know how the minister today can say: "Do not ask me any questions". He still works for him. He evidently has confidence in him today. He must have had confidence in those days.
The relationship between ministers and personal staff is not like departmental relationships. The minister is absolutely responsible for his staff. Nobody selects them but the minister.
It is just like when I was a lawyer. In my firm, I was not always there. When a document was delivered to my office by a bailiff I might not have been there to receive it, but the minute the bailiff put the document in my office, I cannot go in front of the court the week after and say: "I am not responsible" because the bailiff said a document had been put in the office of Mr. Chretien, or the firm of Chretien-Landry-Duchesnes or Lang-Mi-chener, or whatnot. I do not want to make publicity for anybody. The document belongs to me at that minute. If I have a deadline to meet, unless it is something of which I am sure the deadline has expired, I do not get up and say: "Sorry, I was not advised. You gave it to my secretary". That is not an excuse. It is certified that your office has received the documents. We have known some
Supply
lawyers who had to pay big sums of money because documents were misplaced.
The minister said today: "Do not blame me. Do not attack me". Why? I never ran away from being attacked. I never got up in the House of Commons and said: "I am the first French Canadian to be Minister of Finance. Leave me alone. I might look bad. Poor little me, I am the first one. Suppose I fail, there will never be another one". I never said that. I took it on the nose. That is why I have a broken nose today. I replied in kind.
I do not understand, but it is quite evident that he feels terribly uncomfortable, just by the way he acted in the House. It is for them to decide. We cannot. I know that when we form the government, ministers will know. Twenty-five years from now we may train a New Democrat to be a responsible Prime Minister, but not before that.
