speakeroldname: Mr. Benno Friesen (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there have been many surprising twists and turns in this affair, commonly known as the Al-Mashat affair. The first surprise is that he was here. Obviously Canadians were not only surprised; they were shocked. There were a number of other revelations and surprises that came along the way as the committee met, not the least of which was the fact that the assistant under-secretary said in committee, emphasized in committee, how important it was for him always to put things in writing. He liked to do things in writing. He said: "I do not like to do it by phone. You don't remember phone calls, but you always have it on record when you put it in writing". That is what the assistant under-secretary of state said in

June 12, 1991
Supply
committee. But there is not one scrap of paper on this case that he signed, not one scrap of paper.
How do you put the two together? It is surprising to me how that man can sit in committee and say he did more than necessary and yet there is no paper trail. How do you put the two together?
The biggest surprise for most Canadians who have been watching-and I doubt that as many people have watched this event as the opposition thinks-is the resurrection and the rebirth of the rat pack. We remember when the rat pack was bom about seven years ago. Soon after the 1988 election a group of opposition MPs decided they were going to be the rat pack and they attacked ferociously. They did not care what they said. They did not care what kind of indignities they expressed, but they attacked.
It was not long until the people of Canada started asking two important questions. Where is the Leader of the Opposition in this? Either he knows and approves, or he knows, does not approve, but cannot do anything about it.
Now that we have the resurrection of the rat pack, sooner or later Canadians are going to say the same thing about the leader today. We have the rat pack carrying on and yelling all kinds of indecencies and pretty soon-

speakerposition: Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: Indecencies?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That's right. You were not in committee.
Pretty soon Canadians are going to ask if the Leader of the Opposition of today approves of the way these people are carrying on, or does he recognize it and does not approve but cannot do anything about it. If anything has happened as a result of this we have seen a process of the rat pack destroying the present leadership.
We know that the former leader was a decent and honourable man and he did not approve, but he could not control those people. We know the same thing is true about this man. He is a decent and honourable man and it is going to dawn on the Canadian people very quickly that these people are uncontrollable and sooner or later it will bring disrepute on the leadership of the Leader of the Opposition.
We have a motion before us and as the government House leader has already said, we see nothing wrong with this motion. It states the obvious. In fact it was enunciated by people long before this motion came along and we approve of it. Essentially it deals with ministerial responsibility and it looks as though everybody in the House is in favour of it. But, seemingly, everybody has a different definition of it and everybody has a different time when they want to invoke it.
I want to go back as others have done to the McGrath report. I served on that committee as did the member for Papineau-Saint-Michel and, I might add, he served very well as did the member for Winnipeg Transcona. I want to read into the record exactly what the McGrath report says on page 21:
The idea of a minister being responsible for everything that goes on in a department may once have been realistic, but it has long since ceased to be so. A minister cannot possibly know everything that is going on in a department. The doctrine of ministerial accountability undermines the potential for genuine accountability on the part of the person that ought to be accountable-the senior officer of the department.
Clearly the McGrath committee was saying that if we take the view which some of the members today are taking, we relieve officials of the department of then-responsibility and that is not serving Parliament nor the Canadian people.
Therefore the recommendation is:
We recommend that all ministers co-operate with committees exercising their expanded mandates by making available public servants that may be called to testify before a committee.
That is what the McGrath committee said. I think, given different times, members of the House tend to agree with that. It is all well and good to agree with a ministerial responsibility and a statement on that in the heady summer days of parliamentary reform, but it is a little bit more difficult to agree with it when we are facing a winter of discontent.
The fact is that sooner or later we have to make this principle operate and that is what we have been trying to do and that is what the ministers have been trying to do. The Secretary of State for External Affairs stood in the House and said: "We have taken full responsibility". The doctrine of ministerial responsibility says: "We will examine what has gone wrong. We will deal with the public servants. We will correct the mistakes. We will bring in a new regime". That is ministerial responsibility.

What the opposition seems to want is for heads to roll; only it wants ministerial heads to roll, but that is not what the doctrine says. It is not what Former leader of the member for Winnipeg-St. James, said. "When there is a mistake in the department ministerial heads do not necessarily roll", Mr. Trudeau said, as was read into the record earlier by the government House leader.
Just say I made a mistake.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That is right. Just say it was a mistake. There have been mistakes made. They were not made by the minister. How can you make a mistake when you do not even know what happened? I say to my friend from Montreal, how do you know? Members from her party and from the New Democratic Party have all admitted that the ministers did not know. How do you correct it if you do not know?
The motion today and the McGrath committee conform to the common practice of ministerial responsibility. One of the things we have acknowledge is that when you invoke ministerial responsibility, you also include the delegation of responsibility and if that minister is responsible surely that minister can delegate. If the minister delegates, they can hold that person responsible for the way they have carried out their duties. I think the member from Montreal will agree with that. It seems logical.
The business community out there understands that in a company, if the president delegates responsibility to the vice-president and the vice-president delegates it to the manager and the manager boots it, the manager is going to take responsibility and the vice-president is going to take him to account. Now it sees nothing wrong with that.
Out there, the public understands. It has seized that issue and it understands it. The public for the life of it cannot understand why people in the House here are questioning that when there is a mistake made all of a sudden a different regime comes into play. No, we cannot touch people who made mistakes, that would be touching the bureaucracy. We cannot hold them responsible, can we? The public is mystified by what is going on here.
Supply
When ministers delegate responsibilities, they have a right to demand performance. When that performance is not there, they have the right to demand an accounting. That is the process which the ministers have followed throughout this regime.
As I said, the business community understands this. The journalists understand this. This case came to the public attention because a journalist in Toronto called the external affairs department to alert it of an individual who might want to be a defector. It was a journalist.
After that journalist called external affairs, there were public panel discussions on television. There was public discussion in the printed media. There were editorial columns written about whether it was proper for a journalist who presumes to be speaking for the masses or for the newspaper to pay particular attention to one case. Should he plead or lobby on behalf of one person? Was there an impropriety on the part of that one journalist?
There was public discussion for a few days, maybe a week, on that. It is funny, but that person has already been taken out of that job. He is no longer the editor of that newspaper.
The press says: "Of course, it had nothing to do with the Al-Mashat affair". Wink, wink, nudge, nudge. "It had nothing to do with that". It is funny how the timing coincided.
He is on another assignment.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yes. He is already out of that office. I am informing my friend from Montreal that the member is no longer editor of The Financial Post.
Newspapers understand it. They know that you cannot be talking for the public and then lobbying for one. You cannot be speaking for the newspaper and lobby for one. You are accountable to the publisher. They understand it, and he is gone.
He has some other kind of a job, presumably in the newspaper. What I cannot understand for the life of me is why journalists understand it when it is one of their own but not when it is in the government.

Supply
Here we have roughly 40 ministers of the Crown. We have a bureaucracy of 250,000, a quarter of a million. Somehow people in the opposition and some journalists seem to think that 40 ministers ought to keep track of
250,000	bureaucrats. It is not logical. It makes no sense and it violates the whole concept of accountability which bureaucrats want to see.
I do not understand why the opposition cannot understand that. As I pointed out before in the question and answer period, Premier Rae of Ontario understands it very well now that he is in government. While he was in opposition he probably did not. Now that he is in government, he is saying something entirely different.
Now he is saying: "The opposition talks about ministerial responsibility. I have looked into the precedents and there is not a case that I can find in the last 50 years in which a minister was expected to take the wrap, the fall, because something was done without him knowing about it. It is not the ministers who resign. They deal with the people who are the subordinates. They make sure the systems work and they make sure the employees work". That is ministerial responsibility.
I have one further point, and it has to do with the minister's statement. The Secretary of State for External Affairs appeared in committee and she read an eight-page document in which she outlined carefully ministerial responsibility.
She said, from page 4: "Public servants are responsible to the ministers. They advise ministers and administer the programs carried out under the statutory authorities exercised by the ministers. Those ministers, in turn, are responsible to the House of Commons. Officials do, of course, support ministers in answering the committee of the House provided this does not draw officials into partisan controversy or undermine the authority and the responsibility of the ministers".
That is the point, the key point. Officials come before the committees and they come with the ministers, provided it does not draw officials into partisan controversy or undermine the authority of their responsibility to their ministers.
We had a case last week in committee where the minister came before the committee with her officials. She read this statement and at the conclusion she said this: "Now, to place this case in the context of Canada's over-all immigration process, Mr. Kroeger will describe how that process works in all cases, and Mr. Marchand will review the key factual highlights of this particular case and the changes to the procedures that have been
made since then. Then Mr. Valcourt and I will be pleased to respond to questions".
I want to tell my friend from Montreal that when the Secretary of State for External Affairs said: "The officials will now elaborate", members opposite walked out.
That is false.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The member for Burnaby-Kingsway was the first to stand. The member from Winnipeg followed him, as the rest of the committee did. They walked out. I am telling members opposite they cannot have ministerial responsibility both ways. If officials are going to be responsible to the minister, they have to be held responsible to the minister. If these officials come with a minister to a committee, they are under the authority of the minister.
I think that is logical. I think the members will accept that. They are under the authority of the minister and the minister is responsible for them. What the members wanted to do was to draw them out separately and make these public servants accountable not to the minister, but to the committee. There was nothing wrong, and the minister made it a point to underscore the fact that the officials from her department were going to be available to report to the committee.
There is a difference between reporting to a committee, imparting information to a committee, and being responsible to the committee. They cannot have it both ways. They say they want the ministers to be responsible, responsible for the Public Service, how they behave, how they produce and how they perform, but at the same time want them to be responsible to the committee. They cannot do that. Sooner or later they are going to have to make a choice.
It so happened that at that time they got a 30-second or a 60-second clip on television by walking out and having this high dudgeon outside in front of the television. They sacrificed the very principle they said they were working for: holding ministers accountable. As soon as they rejected that opportunity, they were saying: "We want them to be accountable to us and not to the minister".
Were you there, Benno?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I was there. These people have a choice to make. If they really believe in parliamentary and ministerial responsibility, they will take the committee work seriously. They will hold the minister accountable for the way the officials do their work and they will insist that the ministers hold those public servants accountable. If one of them says he would like to put it on record, he would like to put everything on record so that people can read it and so there is a record, but never writes

anything down so there is no paper trail, surely the minister has a right to ask what happened to that official.
It is not an unfair question to ask, is it? If he says he does not like to use a telephone except in an emergency but he wants to put it on record, maybe we have a right to look for those memos which are not there, especially if his boss is travelling in the Middle East and does not know what is happening here.
I want to make one more point and that is the famous so-called secret memo, copies of which are floating all over the place, dated March 7, rewritten on March 8, kept the original date, rewritten again on Monday and did not arrive until March 14. It was written by Mr. Vincent and it was addressed to Ms. McCallion, not to the minister. It was not addressed to the minister and the member for Winnipeg is so upset because this very important secret document did not get to the minister, was not even addressed to him.
It was not even addressed to him and yet he gets into this synthetic rage because something has gone wrong here.
We believe in this motion. We may not be able to vote for it because of the conventions of this House but we believe in the motion, and we have performed according to the demands of this motion as the ministers can prove.

Mr. Speaker, I listened carefully to the hon. member's comments on ministerial responsibility. I am even prepared to go along with part of his comments, to the extent that the minister or ministers said they had not been informed.
How can we in this House and how can Canadians believe that at a time when we were at war with a country an ambassador of this calibre was not under surveillance by CSIS and our country's security agencies, that no one
Supply
was aware of his activities and that he was able to enter a country like Canada? This is not a banana republic. He entered Canada. How can we believe that no one knew about it?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am glad the member asked that question because it underscores exactly the problem that we have been discussing in committee.
The first telephone call came on February 27. It came to the Assistant Under-Secretary of State. He did not bother calling the minister. What he did do was place a call to Vienna and alert Vienna that there was somebody who might come and want to defect, but he did not tell the minister upstairs. I think it was the next day the minister was going to Washington to meet with Baker and talk about Middle East issues. He let him go to Washington and did not tell him that somebody from Iraq was wanting to defect to Canada. He let it go by way of memos and discussions. Nothing, there was not one memo written to alert and warrant a response from the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
General memos, yes. None of them said: "for the attention of", "we want a response", "we want to have some direction from the minister".
I will tell you why. A week prior to that two ministers had said: "There is a case coming before us, another diplomat from Iraq. He should have no special privileges".
They knew what the attitude of the minister was on this. He wants to know how this happened and I will tell you why. It all was steamrolled by the security division of external affairs. I am not saying this is inviolate. I am not saying that it was trying to do something tawdry, not at all. It was looking after what it thought were the best interests of an individual who felt that he was in danger. I think we have to get it out of our minds that it was trying to do something tawdry.

June 12, 1991

The security division checks on whether this person is there was no malice and there was no intent to conspire really a defector. The word comes back that he is not or do anything wrong. Would you agree with that? considered a defector.
It deals with an immigration officer in Vienna. Vienna reports back to external affairs. It was never reported directly back to the immigration department. Never did a telex go directly from Vienna to the immigration department here, it always went to external affairs. By March 11 it was case closed. They had been provisionally accepted on March 5, the day after the first interview.
Mrs. Al-Mashat came in on the evening of March 4. Mr. Al-Mashat came in on March 5 and both were provisionally accepted at the interview, providing their medicals and their security checks were okay. The security division made sure that it checked out that section.
Also you mentioned a few moments ago in your first remarks a comment about Mr. Trudeau's statement in 1983 with regard to ministerial responsibility. I would like you to elaborate on that a little more if you could. That was an interesting comment and I would like to hear your thoughts on that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the issue of fairness, I do not think that we can blow it out of proportion in terms of looking after what went wrong. That has to be taken care of. The minister has done that. We are dealing with human individuals and therefore things can go wrong, but we have to guarantee for Canadians as far as humanly possible that we will conduct a fair operation so that everybody across Canada gets the same treatment.
It was a quick adoption of the process. It was not illegal. It was, I think, improper, but it was not illegal and because the system was made to function extra efficiently these people got in while thousands of people around the world wanted to get in. It was terribly unfair. I want to underscore that the officials did nothing legally or technically wrong. They thought they were doing right, but it was wrong.
In that sense it is not overblown. In the sense of the publicity, yes it is overblown. The Secretary of State for External Affairs has said that she has in the meantime gone to Chile and dealt with incredible issues with the Organization of American States to ensure that becomes a more active and a viable union on behalf of North and South America, and maybe deal with some of the poverty issues and the security issues that face this hemisphere.

Mr. Speaker, I just wondered in the opinion of the hon. member if this does not appear to be blown out of all proportion. It seems to me that we are occupying an awful lot of our time here in Question Period and in the House today on this issue months after it has happened.
When I call back to the people in the riding and I ask "are you concerned about this" or "are you following this", I do not find that people in my riding are following it closely at all. There were some questions in the beginning and, as you just said, a lot of people who did have relatives and friends whom they wanted to have come to Canada and who have been working hard at it for years who perhaps were very disappointed to see this happen. I agree with that. In all fairness, however, is it not blown out of all proportion considering the fact that, as you said, there was no malice? Perhaps there was a difference of opinion in the judgment used, and I think that is true. Perhaps there were some mistakes made, but
She has been to Copenhagen and she has been dealing with NATO issues; whether we ought to change the relationship within NATO. She has met with NATO foreign ministers. That has incredibly long range implications for our country. None of this gets any attention as long as we are dealing with "where is that secret memo". That is the destructive part of this debate. There is nothing wrong with holding ministers accountable, nothing wrong with making sure that the system remains fair. That is the way it ought to be, but it is wrong to distort the issue to such an extent that the issues which face our country and the world get completely obliterated and blotted out by this one issue, in order to get a few seconds of a television clip.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I have two minutes left in question or comment period. I will recognize the hon. member for Mount Royal for a minute and then have a rebuttal for a minute.

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank my hon. colleague very much for addressing many of his remarks this way.
The issue of the memo is important, if I may suggest to my hon. colleague, because it is not an ordinary memo. The memo was dealing with a man that my colleague and I have talked about in international meetings, a really unpleasant, not very good, dictator in Iraq with whom we were at war. I think you could say that this man we were referring to, Al-Mashat, was an apologist for him.
If it was just an ordinary piece of paper or just an ordinary memo, I guess we could have said was, perhaps pushing the case a little bit too far. But this was not an ordinary memo. I would suggest that you should not distort it in that regard.
Second, like you and like most members in this House, we have hundreds and hundreds of immigration and refugee cases. I do not have to tell you, because you and I have discussed this, the number of married men over here who have not had the pleasure of being able to live and have their wives, and some of them their children here, for over three years because they cannot get through this refugee and immigration system.
When you read the minister's statement and she was bringing the members of her staff before the committee to discuss the process and the procedure, I think that was logical. We got lots of things to look at there and we have lots of reasons to be angry that this man, Al-Mashat, apologist for Saddam Hussein, was in here. There is good reason.

Mr. Speaker, just to put it on the record, I will be taking 10 minutes of

I would like to look at this entire issue from the point of view of two words; honesty and integrity. First of all, I look at precisely what we are talking about. In general terms we are talking about ministerial responsibility.
My colleague from Winnipeg South Centre moved a very specific motion. Lest the people who are watching and who will read Hansard not know, they may wonder where in heaven's name did this wording come from.
I would like everyone to know that the wording is verbatim, extracted from the white paper on the future of the Public Service which was tabled on the Prime Minister's behalf on December 12, 1990, and which was quoted favourably by the Secretary of State for External Affairs when she appeared before the Al-Mashat committee. Why is that important?
It is important because that statement is a statement of principle by this government of ministerial responsibility. Among other things it says that ministers are responsible to this House and through this House to Canadians for the activities of government and individually, and I quote:
Ministers are responsible for the administration of the decisions of
the Government and the activities of Public Servants falling under
their jurisdiction;
That is a principle with which the members of the government do not have a quarrel, or so we are told. Indeed it would be very illogical if they did have a quarrel with it since their own minister quoted it favourably. However, how does it apply to situations like the Al-Mashat affair? That really is the key.
I thought in the time allotted to me I would just have a look at the calendar of events. Members on the opposite side are interested in history when it suits their purposes. I would like to deal with some facts.
Factually, let us go back to 1984. We will all remember that the Prime Minister of today, then the Leader of the Opposition, campaigned long and hard on the issues of honesty and integrity and on the faith that people should have in the government and on the faith that he would redeliver to people when he became Prime Minister. Unfortunately that has not happened and people are very disappointed. This Al-Mashat affair would have been and still can be a perfect opportunity for this government to rekindle faith in the political process with Canadians, to reinstill a feeling of honesty and integrity.

June 12, 1991
Supply

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to speak on the most fundamental principle underlying our system of responsible government, the constitutional responsibility of ministers.
Recent events, of which we in this House are all aware, have given rise to considerable comment from members of Parliament-as we see here today and in Question Period in the past few weeks-the public and the media about the nature and practice of this principle. Indeed the motion which we are debating shows that interest in this principle is alive and as well in this Parliament as it should be.
I wish to first address the motion itself. On its face it is a very straightforward motion calling upon members of Parliament to announce their support for the doctrine of ministerial responsibility. The vehicle being used, as is conceded by the Liberal Party opposite, is a non-confidence motion. Were it to pass, it would require the government to resign.

However, we on the government side of the House can hardly accept this as a straightforward attempt on the part of the Liberal Party to encourage non-partisan all-party support for the principles underlying this doctrine to which this government has adhered faithfully in recent events.
It is a political ploy to embarrass the government. That is all it is. Let me therefore set out for this House the nature and elements of the doctrine of ministerial responsibility.
Ministers exercise powers bestowed on them by the Crown in Parliament and hold office at the pleasure of the Crown. The exercise of these powers, for which ministers are constitutionally responsible to Parliament, provides the foundation of responsible government.
The concentration of responsibility in the hands of ministers reflects the fundamental democratic principle that the power of the state must be exercised under the authority of elected officials accountable to the representatives of the electorate.
This enables Parliament to focus responsibility for the conduct of government on those of its members who hold ministerial office and who ultimately must personally answer to Parliament and hence to the electorate for their actions and the actions of their subordinates.
Ministers fulfil their responsibilities and are called to account by the House of Commons, for the exercise of their statutory authority in accordance with practice and convention. From the origins of our system, however, political circumstances rather than literal application of the principle of ministerial responsibility have governed the answerability of ministers. As Professor J. R. Mallory has noted, the minister's is a political responsibility.
What that means is that it is a political, policy setting responsibility. It is not a day-to-day administrative responsibility of the running of that department. Deputy ministers derive almost all of their authority from ministers. They advise ministers and administer the programs carried out under the statutory authorities exercised by their ministers. The tradition is that they are loyal to their ministers and are required actively to support and participate in the policy and administrative decisions taken by ministers individually and collectively.

Put simply, deputy ministers are responsible to their ministers and are accountable to them.
Deputy ministers also support their ministers in answering to committees of the House provided this does not draw officials into partisan controversy or undermine the authority and responsibility of ministers. This role of officials has been enhanced and strengthened by the McGrath report which recommended that public servants be made more available to parliamentary committees. The government stated at the time that it supported this recommendation and recent events have borne out the government's commitment in this regard.
The concentration of responsibility in the hands of ministers is obviously the bedrock of parliamentary government. It is, however, a matter of observation that government is a large administrative enterprise. It is very important to recognize that it is not a modern phenomenon that ministers cannot know everything that is done under their authority. The phenomenon is merely more acute today than it was a century ago, and not prima facie proof of the irrelevance of ministerial responsibility. Ministers spend much of their time providing information to Parliament, indicating a need for the minister's ability to answer and provide information to be shared without however sharing his or her responsibility.
Professor Kenneth Kernaghan has noted: "It is now almost universally accepted that it is unreasonable to hold a minister personally responsible in the form of resignation for the administrative failings of his subordinates. The usual practice is that the minister informs Parliament that the fault lies with his officials and he promises that the offenders will be disciplined and their mistakes corrected. Despite frequent calls by opposition parties for ministerial resignations on the grounds of actual or alleged departmental mismanagement, in practice, ministers in cabinet do not resign as penance for administrative bungling in their department".
Professor Geoffrey Marshall, a leading British authority, sums up the doctrine and practice of ministerial responsibility as follows: "When action is taken of which a minister disapproves and", here is the more appropriate part, "of which he has not prior knowledge, there is no obligation on his part to endorse it, to defend the errors of his officials, or to resign".

Mr. Speaker, a former cabinet colleague of mine in the Dave Barrett administration, Ernie Hall, when something went wrong in our government, once quoted what he called a Limey proverb to the effect that if something happens once it is happenstance. If there is a second happening that is a coincidence. If it happens three times then somebody is managing the affair.

June 12, 1991
Supply
The hon. member from Kitchener has described a litany of events which all conspired together to make sure that none of the cabinet members knew about this incident, this case, this person who wanted to come in.
We are asked to believe not one, not two, not three happenings but a whole litany of events conspired together to make it possible. It is difficult to believe. I am not saying it is not the truth, but I am saying it is very difficult to believe.
As I say, twice is coincidence. Third is getting unbelievable. When it gets to 13 and 33 then we have to wonder if somebody is not managing the events.
The question was asked earlier in the debate: "Are we not dealing with this out of all proportion to the importance of the case?" I am inclined to agree with that.
Certainly I am as concerned as other members are about the way in which one person was able to jump the queue in the way that person did. I must have close to 100 open files in my office where people have been trying to get admission to Canada. Some of them are from as long ago as the election of 1988. They still have not completed the process, yet this one particular person was able to do it within 28 days.
Had one of the 100 or so who concern me right now managed to jump the queue then I would say: Yes, something went wrong. The system broke down. It was just too easy compared to all the rest.
When a very high profile person such as this jumps the queue then I have to wonder. I cannot say all these people are not telling the truth, but I really have to wonder whether it is possible for all those events to come together. It was not just a casual person brought in out of all the people who want to immigrate into Canada. It is this one particular person who from all the rest is the fortunate recipient of all of these happy events which combined together to make sure that he was able to enter Canada legally.
It strains the bounds of credibility. I have a great deal of difficulty in believing that it could be so easy for one high profile person with a well-known name when none of the people with whom I am dealing can find a way of getting in even within the regular time.
Having said that, I still think we are spending more time on this than it is worth. The part that bothers me-I
have highlighted just a few words in the motion introduced by the Official Opposition-is that ministers are responsible for the activities of public servants falling under their jurisdiction.
I was a cabinet minister, and I certainly believe that. It does not apply just to cabinet ministers. You can recall the Leader of the Opposition in his speech talking about his experience as a lawyer. If someone delivered a document to my office-I ran an accounting business until some time after the election when I had to give up that part of my life-even had I been away on vacation, it was still my responsibility. If the client came in and complained about me losing something that belonged to him or her, I would not go to my staff and try to find out which one it was and then tell the client that it was so-and-so on my staff. I would want to know. I would want to find out who received it. I would want to trail it and see if I could not find it or have them find it, but there is certainly no point in me telling the client who was to blame. I had the responsibility.
For a while in my life I was a poultry farmer, an egg producer. Eggs have to be candled to check the interior quality as well as examining the exterior. I did not lay the eggs, but if a customer complained to me about the quality of one of those eggs that I was selling him there was no point in me blaming the chicken, finding out which hen laid it and saying that she was to blame. I was responsible. I was the proprietor and it was my responsibility.
In the same way the cabinet minister is responsible. I was a cabinet minister and I had problems in my department. It never once occurred to me to find out who the offending individual was with a view to telling people outside my ministry who that person was and what he or she had done wrong. I was the one who was responsible. I suppose, in different circumstances, President Truman said it in less than 20 minutes, much shorter and very concise: "The buck stops here".
I was the minister of that department and it was my responsibility. Things did go wrong and I wanted to find out who and why and to try to set in motion procedures to make sure that those same things did not go wrong again, and I never had that third happening. Sometimes a coincidence but never to the point where I was suspicious of the whole process. That is the cabinet minister's responsibility.
June 12, 1991

In this instance we are led to believe, as I say, that cabinet ministers did not know. Four of them who have been identified in debates in this House, should have known something about it. There was a paper trail and they should have known. In some cases it was suggested they did not get around to reading their mail. A lot of us do not get around to reading our mail, but if it is important mail we see it and we see it promptly. If not, we want to find out why not.
If there is someone in our office who has not done his or her job properly, we have a way of dealing with that person. Depending upon the severity and depending on the incident, there are different ways of dealing with it. But it would certainly never occur to me to blame one of my staff members if a constituent was not served properly or if the job was not done correctly. I do not do it all and none of us can. We all have help to do our work, but we are responsible for everything that goes out of our offices and everything that is done in our constituency offices.
Not often but occasionally we do get some credit. If there is any blame we cannot pass it on to anyone else. It is our blame and it is our responsibility.
That is the way it has to be in cabinet. Public servants and public employees do not have any way of speaking out. If they do, it is cause for dismissal. When public servants were named in this case, individuals named before the committee started meeting and before they started getting into the evidence, those individuals were named. That is not fair to people who do not have any voice. They can speak to their minister. They can speak to the person to whom they are responsible, but they have no right to say anything outside the minister's office about anything that has happened. They have taken an oath not to.
There is responsibility and there is loyalty.
The people working with the minister have to be loyal to him or her. Otherwise they do not belong there and they had better find another job. The minister has to demand loyalty. He cannot afford to have that person going out and cutting the ground out from under his feet under any circumstance.
I had that happen to me just once. The offending person said that he was just joking and did not mean it seriously, but it never happened a second time to anyone in the department. The person was not fired, but

certainly the message got around that kind of conduct was not acceptable.
On the other hand, nobody in my ministry ever had to worry that I was not supporting them. If anything went wrong then I would have it out with that person, but it never occurred to me to say publicly that somebody in my department had done something wrong or that it was not my fault if things were not done right: in other words, that I did everything right but some individuals whom I would name were the ones who did everything wrong.
It does not work that way. That is not acceptable. The public has a right to know who is responsible. The premier or Prime Minister has the right to know who is responsible and not to have to blame a public servant or anyone else. Before resuming debate, I am now in a position to make a ruling regarding the motion put forward by the hon. member for Nanaimo -Cowichan.
His amendment is out of order on two counts. First, it introduces a concept irrelevant to the main motion and, on this point, I refer to Beauchesne's sixth edition, citation 579(1), which says: "An amendment setting forth a proposition dealing with a matter which is foreign to the proposition involved in the main motion is not relevant and cannot be moved".
Second, in Beauchesne's sixth edition again, citation 929 states:

"On an allotted day, during consideration of the business of supply, an amendment must not provide the basis for an entirely different debate than that proposed in the original motion".

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to speak on the most fundamental principle underlying our system of responsible government, the constitutional responsibility of ministers.
Recent events of which we in this House are all aware have given rise to considerable comment from members of Parliament, the public and the media about the nature and practice of this principle.
Indeed the motion we are debating shows that interest in this principle is alive and well in this Parliament. I may add that some of the comments on ministerial responsibility we have heard and read in recent weeks contain a number of misconceptions which have helped confuse the issue instead of explain how this doctrine was applied in Canada.
I welcome the opportunity to speak on this subject today. I hope to provide some clarification for members of this House and the Canadian public and address some of the key elements of this fundemental principle of our democratic system of government.
I wish to first address the motion itself. On its face it is very straightforward motion calling upon members of Parliament to announce their support for the doctrine of ministerial responsibility.
The vehicle being used, as is conceded by the Liberal Party opposite in the debate on a previous supply motion on medicare, is a non-confidence motion.
Were it to pass, it would require the government to resign. But we on the government side of the House can hardly accept this as a straightforward attempt on the part of the Liberal Party to encourage non-partisan, all-party support for the principles underlying the doctrine to which this government has adhered faithfully in recent events.
Let me therefore set out for this House the nature and elements of the doctrine of ministerial responsibility. Minister exercise powers bestowed on them by the Crown in Parliament thus providing the foundation of responsible government, and under the Constitution they are accountable to Parliament for their actions and the actions of their officials.
The concentration of responsibility in the hands of ministers reflets the fundamental democratic principle that the power of the state must be exercised under the authority of elected officials accountalbe to the representatives of the electorate. Public servants, in turn, are accountable to the ministers. They advise them and administer the programs implemented by virtue of the powers exercised by the ministers.
Former Auditor General Kenneth Dye was fond of saying that some public servants knew what was going on in their departments but ministers did not because the machine had become top unwieldy.
These powers are therefore conferred on ministers by Parliament, and ministers are accountable to the House of Commons.
Public servants also support their ministers in aswering to committees of the House, provided this does not draw officials into partisan controversy or undermine the authority and responsibility of ministers.
June 12, 1991

Ministers fulfil their responsibility and are called to account by the Elouse of Commons for the exercise of their statutory authority in accordance with practice and convention. As Professor J. R. Mallory has noted, the minister's is a political responsibility.
It is, however, a matter of observation that governe-ment is a large administrative enterprise. It is not a modern phenomenon that ministers cannot know everything that is done under their authority. The phenomenon is merely more acute today than it was before.
How ministers deal with their responsibility for their officials depends on the circumstances and whether, for instance, an official took action that was totally unacceptable, without the minister's knowledge. Of course if the minister was not informed he cannot be responsible.
Briefly here are the essential components of this doctrine. Authority is conferred by the Crown and exercised by ministers who are accountable to Parliament.
Ministers are responsible for the actions of their officials whether they did or did not know what those actions were. When a mistake is made without the minister's knowledge the minister must establish the facts, correct the mistake and make sure it does not happen again. The minister informs the House of the steps taken.
From what I can see, precedents at the federal level in Canada support this interpretation of the doctrine. Professor Kenneth Kemaghan, in an article entitled Power, Parliament and Public Servants in Canada: Ministerial Responsibility Reexamined published in Canadian Public Policy, volume 3, 1979, noted: "It is now almost universally accepted that it is unreasonable to hold a minister personally responsible in the form of resignation for the administrative failings of subordinates." It is on page 36.
The usual practice is that the minister informs Parliament that the fault lies with his officials and promises that the offenders will be disciplined and their mistakes corrected. That is on page 387.
Private Members' Business
Professor Kemaghan also said: "Despite frequent calls by opposition parties for ministerial resignations on the grounds of actual or alleged departmental mismanagement, in practice in Canada ministers in cabinet do not resign as pennace for administrative bungling in their department". This quote is from page 386.
Addressing the same issue in a book entitled Ministerial Responsibility, Oxford, 1989, Professors S. E. Finer and Geoffrey Marshall, both leading British authorities on the subject, sum up the doctrine and practice of ministerial responsibility as follows: "When we refer to the individual ministerial responsibility we simply mean that for any action taken by or omission on the part of a civil servant, a minister or someone else is expected to provide information to Parliament. This, only ministers can do". "When action is taken of which a minister disapproves and of which he has no prior knowledge, there is no obligation on his part to endorse it, to defend the errors of his officials, or to resign", said Marshall at page 386.
Applying the doctrine just outlined in some reform to the facts of the Al-Mashat case, I would note the following. First, ministers did not know anything of the Al-Mashat affair until after Al-Mashat had entered Canada legally.
Second, when they were informed they took full responsibility by acting to establish the facts.
Third, when the facts were established they took appropriate action to ensure there would be no repetition and they sought an apology from those involved.
Fourth, ministers informed the House of how they had their responsibilities.
Fifth, given the ministers' commitment to a thorough investigation and to making the facts public, and given the findings of the investigation and the nature of the report flowing therefrom, it became inevitable that the identity of the officials principally involved would obviously become public.
Given the political and constitutional history of Canada, we have to conclude that this government has acted according to the above-mentioned principles and doctrine because since Confederation no minister has had to resign due to an error made by a public servant.

June 12, 1991
Private Members' Business
I have talked at length about the doctrine of ministerial responsibility and its direct application in this case, as suggested in the motion. I have no doubt hon. members will acknowledge that this government, through its recent efforts, has fully abided by this doctrine.

June 12, 1991

believe that, from a psychological point of view, this would be highly significant for Canadians and the economy. The GST has had a negative impact. When you look at the number of people crossing the border to shop in the United States, you get an idea of the degree of rejection of this new tax by the public. Mr. Speaker, if you look at the statistics for the last few months, you will notice a very negative reaction on the part of Canadians. Indeed, the government had said many times in this House that the price of several products would go down. But that has not been the case, except perhaps for automobiles. We have not seen any price reduction in several kinds of businesses. Whether it was hardware, clothing or any other product, there has been no reduction. So it was unthinkable to believe that in the over-all Canadian economy there would be a price reduction on all products on which the manufacturers' sales tax had been applied, that businesses would reduce their prices, that the GST would be applied and that we would save money. It is not the case at all.

The motion I brought before the House concerns the goods and services tax, the GST. It is not only an extremely major tax increase, it has had a psychological effect. All you have to do is check the figures to see how the retail sales took a dramatic drop in many sectors of our economy.
There is no doubt there was a reaction, be it crossborder shopping or a reduction in consumer spending. We would have to say not only is there a reduction in consumer spending but the amount of money we have had to spend has been curbed substantially. If you take into consideration all these factors, the GST has done great damage to the economy.
Private Members' Business
At the time when we felt the economy was slowing down, that we were going into a recession, it seems that common sense should have dictated that there should have been a delay at least of the GST.
The effects were detrimental and they are compounding. There were alternatives to the whole affair. Figures do not lie and we are seeing the results.
If you take the fact that there was an alternative solution for the way we tax our people, we consider that the government could have found a simpler way of finding additional revenue without penalizing the whole country and affecting the economy to the point that we are into a recession. It took them many weeks to admit that we are into a recession.
In the literature that has been written on the subject, everybody who is aware of global economics has reported that the tax burden has increased substantially in this country. They summed it up in this way, and I could not find better words: "At the risk of over-simplification, my assessment of the Tory tax change is summarized in this fashion."
He says: "It is less equitable and more complicated. The corporate tax increase has improved their position. It is a more stable and predictable source of revenue. It is more neutral and hence more efficient." That is corporate tax. It went down. It says here that basically the GST has turned out to be quite complicated, and a large number of small businesses that never had to deal with the manufacturers' sales tax were the big losers in this whole affair along with the Canadian people.
What I contend is that it does not take a degree in economics to realize that basic common sense is always the best answer when dealing with anything, even economics.
The major factor is that the government came in with a major tax measure without going into any kind of basic tax reform. The best example of all is New Zealand.
Two years prior to putting in the goods and services tax, it had a major overhaul, a major tax reform. It was quite remarkable. Taxes were lowered considerably. Prior to the GST, it lowered personal income tax substantially-I mean substantially.
Lately I have read that the New Zealand government was not impressed with the way the Canadian government introduced its GST. The New Zealand government realized that public perception was extremely important. It wanted to cover up the loopholes and it wanted it to be a progressive tax.

June 12, 1991
Private Members' Business
Before implementing the GST, it lowered the personal income tax substantially. By doing so, a lot of people in the economy were paying taxes when probably they had not before. If the New Zealand government was highly successful with its transfer, why could we not have taken a cue from it when we were trying to put in the GST.
Basically the whole situation rested upon the fact that the government decided to put tax over tax. Therefore, we are left with a situation where not only are we saturated, but we have signs of a tax revolt on our hands. Of course, the government will not admit it. The figures are there. We know that taxes, direct or indirect, have been put on the Canadian people in the last years. It has been detrimental.
I am not saying that the government is totally responsible. For the last 10 or 15 years we have needed a profound tax reform which we have not had. We have an elite in this country which dictates to our governments. It literally dictates to our governments.
If there is something that is fundamental in a democracy, it is the way we tax our people. Yet we are going along half baked. No research has been done, no political will has been put into our tax system to make sure that it is fair and equitable. How many Canadians feel that the tax system in this country is fair and equitable? None.
We have a gentleman over there. Thank God I do not know your riding and your name because your electors would certainly be on your back. You had better listen to your electors more often.

speechtext: Tell them that you want to tax food like New Zealand. Tell us about the New Zealand tax on food.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   THE CANADIAN ECONOMY REMOVAL OF THE GST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we will excuse him for his ignorance.

As I said, one of the most fundamental elements in a democracy is the way people are taxed. For years, not since this government has been in power, but for at least 10 or 15 years there has been a need for a comprehensive reform of our tax system.
We have a tax system which has become utterly inequitable and unfair. It does not take a degree in economics to realize that changes are imperative. Everywhere in our country people complain that the tax burden has become intolerable, that they have less and less leeway. The middle class is the backbone of a society. If the middle class is overtaxed, how the economy could be sound and progressive? It is impossible.
The goal of the motion that I introduce tonight-and I really do not expect the change to come tomorrow-is that we recognize at least the need for a reform. We must repeat it because the financial elite of our country tells us that everything is as fine as it can be, but it is far from true. If anybody should be knowledgeable in Canada, it is we, because we represent these taxpayers and we are very much aware that they cannot take it any more.
No matter what political party we represent in this House, we are at the limit. People have had enough of the tax system and they want us to have the political will, the courage and the honesty to say: "We want a comprehensive reform of our tax system." If we, who represent the people, are not in a position to recognize the needs and real interests of all Canadians, what exactly is our role in this House?
Are we speaking on behalf of the financial elite in this House, or are we speaking for all Canadians, especially the middle class, the backbone of our society? These are the things we should be discussing among ourselves. We have to recognize that it is essential for Canadians that we bring about a reform. It will never be said often enough.
If the decision makers in the government do not listen to those who represente the nation's 295 ridings, what hope can there be?
With this motion, we hope to start a discussion that will keep on growing. We also want to make sure that all the financial and even the social organizations will recognize the need and that they will keep pressuring those who represent them in this House, to let them know that it is time to consider the interests of all Canadians.



In conclusion, I am amazed sometimes to see the reaction of some of my colleagues across the way. They cannot make me believe that the people in their constituencies do not want to see a reform of the tax system, that they feel it is no longer fair and equitable.
We are not spokesmen here for the financial elite in this country. We are the spokesmen for all Canadians and especially the middle class, which is the backbone of this society. If we cannot have the political courage or the honesty to reflect what the people in this country want from us, what hope is there?
I would like to know where the hope is going to be for the rest of the Canadian people in this country. If there is anything more fundamental in a democracy than the tax system, you tell me what. There are probably two great priorities in this country; the constitutional political issue and the financial problem that we have. Unless we can face up to it there is no hope.

Mr. Speaker, I do not know if my time has expired, but I would ask you to give me a few minutes to sum up.
I think my colleagues opposite should go back to their ridings and poll their constituents. I do not have to tell them what to say; they know. But each and every one of us has a duty to fulfil here. Whatever party we represent in this House, we have individual obligations, and that is to reflect the concerns, especially the material concerns, of Canadians.
That is why I want all Canadians to put pressure on or seek the support of the member who represents them in this House to express their points of view. Together we could convince the government's mandarins, if you like, and say: Listen, we are not asking for miraculous changes, we are asking for a reform of our taxation system. It would be a first step. I am convinced that as soon as we consider a true reform of our taxation system, it will be a sign that we acknowledge the problem we are facing and that we have the courage and the political will to solve it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the short time I have tonight, I am pleased to get an opportunity to speak on this motion which we can certainly support because I think for the first time in some time we actually have a truthful motion coming from the Liberals.
Part of the motion deals with the impact of the goods and services tax on Canadians, as we have learned in the last few days. It was the government's own Department of Finance which last week revealed the contents of the
Private Members' Business
motion, and that is how the government either deliberately or through its usual bungling has shown that the revenues to the government under the GST are considerably higher than they were ever predicted to be.
Net GST revenues totalled $2.2 billion in the first three months of this year, 22 per cent higher than the $1.8 billion the government predicted a few months ago in the 1991 budget. Gross GST revenues, including the GST low income credit, were $2.78 billion. We can see by looking at the motion that is actually the truth of what is happening in our economy because of the goods and services tax which was brought in and rammed through this Parliament by the Conservative government. Business communities, consumers and Canadians all across the country are now facing the trouble in our economy, the recession which is being led by the policies of this government. The recession is being encouraged by the policies of this government in bringing in the goods and services tax.
We had in this House a debate about the goods and services tax, in which the then Minister of Finance said there was no other alternative, there was no other way to go, it was the GST or nothing. "Give us your alternatives", he said, "Tell us what you would do instead".
We certainly heard from the government on how it is driving Canadian consumers into the ground. We also heard from the New Democrats who presented, and we were the only party to do so in this House, a detailed alternative to the goods and services tax. We laid out the plans that we said could raise revenues for government. We could reform the manufacturers' sales tax so that government would have those revenues and be able to implement the programs that Canadians need.
That is why I do not think you can talk about the GST in isolation from the general taxation policies that this government has followed. If you look at some of the policies and ideas that our caucus has put forward, there is plenty of tax revenue out there. The fact is that this government and its friends from the Liberal Party over the years have failed to collect those revenues from the wealthy corporations.

June 12, 1991
Private Members' Business
A graph that was produced with the information from the government's own department is a very revealing one. It clearly shows what all Canadians know, that under the tax policies followed by the Liberals and now the Conservatives, the personal share of income tax has been rising and the corporate share has been declining.
This is a very interesting graph, as is the background material which I would be pleased to send to anyone who is watching and listening to the debate tonight.
I would like to indicate just what this impact means in a community. What does the GST mean to a community such as Prince George? The estimates tell us that the GST will mean that individual Canadians will be paying at least an extra $600 a year. People tell me that is a conservative estimate and that it is likely to be much higher. What that means for a community such as Prince George, with 70,000 people at $600 extra a year is that the Conservative Party of Canada is sucking an extra $42 million out of that community. It is no wonder people are suffering. It is no wonder that businesses in the area, as was indicated earlier this week when we had the debate on youth unemployment, are suffering. They cannot hire those extra students because of the difficulties they are having with the goods and services tax.
In my riding in a community just west of Prince George at Bums Lake there is a gentleman, Mr. Brown, who is really putting his principles on the line. I talked to him on the telephone earlier tonight. He has a small business there called Process 4 and he is not collecting GST. He is not collecting it on principle because he does not believe in the tax. He welcomes the day when the government's tax collectors get around to seeing him and take him to court because he is prepared to fight for what he believes. Not a lot of people will do that but in this case he will and I think he deserves our support for that because in fighting this tax he is certainly living by his principles.
In fact it is an anomaly. He has people who are tourists who have heard about his cause and are dropping into his store deliberately purchasing items from him because he does not charge the GST. You must know, Mr. Speaker, from your own riding, how much Canadians resent this very unfair tax. In fact it tells us that Tory times are taxing times.
I hope that in the next election campaign when the policies of our party go up against the policies of the other parties, it will be very clear to Canadians that the New Democrats stand alone among all of the parties. Even the Reformers are fudging on the GST now-they do not know whether to support it or be against it-and we are never sure where the Liberals stand.
At our recent convention in Halifax there was part of a resolution from my riding wherein we said we would abolish the GST and bring in a fair tax system. When I am back on the doorsteps in that next election campaign, whenever it is held, that is going to be a message we will take to the doorstep. My advice to Canadians from coast to coast to coast is, when those Tories phone-you know how they bother you at suppertime-to try to get you to vote for them, you should ask for your money back. Canadians should tell the Tory canvassers that they want their money back because of the unfair tax policies of this government. At the next election when the New Democrats form the government, we will bring in a fair tax system, fair to all Canadians. We will ensure the revenues are there for government so that we can have the policies and programs we need. We can do nothing more than that.
I call on the government members opposite to get up their courage and support this motion. Their government's own information tells them that the motion is true. Join with the rest of Canadians. Reject the goods and services tax and bring in a fair tax system.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   THE CANADIAN ECONOMY REMOVAL OF THE GST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to participate in this private members' debate and to speak most definitely and vehemently against the motion put by the member for Gatineau-La Lievre.
I am disappointed in the motion, which suggests that government should envisage the removal of the GST and, in keeping with Liberal policy all the way along, offer no alternative.
There is no way this government or any future government is going to envisage eliminating some form of sales tax. I think we learned from the experience of the past 50 years that the old form of federal sales tax, the federal manufacturers' sales tax was fundamentally flawed, was out of step with modern society and simply had to be

replaced with something more up to date. That of course was the genesis of the goods and services tax.
None of the other parties came forward with any workable or viable alternatives. The Liberal Party had nothing whatever to offer and that is still the position of the Liberal Party.
The previous speaker from the New Democratic Party said: "Well, we had all sorts of alternatives". In fairness, they did. As I recall it, flawed as the old federal manufacturers' sales tax was, as bad as it was for Canadian manufacturers, putting them at a disadvantage with imported goods, in spite of all of that and understanding that, the NDP would still have retained that out-moded, out-dated, antiquated tax. They would have brought it back to 9 per cent from 13.5 per cent.
To make up the rest of the revenue which otherwise would have been gathered by the old federal manufacturers' sales tax, the NDP would, of course, have raised other income taxes accordingly and brought back estate tax. What a wonderful thing. It was the NDP in Saskatchewan which had the last estate tax, as I recall it and finally got rid of it in 1977 because it was so grossly unpopular.
The thought that after the toils of a lifetime, after paying income tax year after year, that the bit people could accumulate would be taxed away from them upon their passing is the NDP alternative to the GST.
I am really surprised that the hon. member has brought forward this motion after all we have seen and heard over the past number of months and years with regard to sales tax. It must be that the Liberal position simply never changes.
I recall a few years ago that the then finance critic for the Liberal Party, I believe it was the member for Etobicoke North, was dismissed from his position as the finance critic for the Liberal Party because he spoke the truth. He came forward with an honest assessment when he said: "Of course the deficit is a problem. Of course the deficit that we Liberals created over the last 20 years, the national debt, has to be addressed". He went on to say that there had to be reform of sales tax. For that and some other honest transgressions he was dismissed from his position.
Private Members' Business
It is interesting to note that the party's associate finance critic today, the member for Ottawa South, is quoted in The Toronto Star. We all know that if it is in The Toronto Star it certainly must be gospel, so I will not hestiate to repeat it here.
The current associate finance critic of the hon. member's Liberal Party says the Liberals have simply avoided the question of the deficit, simply accusing the government of mismanaging the nation's finances, but not saying what they would do themselves.
The party's associate finance critic, the member for Ottawa South, says this may work for an opposition party, but it will not convince Canadians that Liberals are capable of governing. He urged his colleagues to make the transition. That was a day or two ago, and it is unfortunate that the member who put the motion that we are now debating did not hear that, because the proposal makes a whole lot of sense.
Unfortunately, the hon. member for Gatineau-La Lievre has fallen into the old Liberal position of ignoring reality. Just do away with the GST, he says, we will not worry about $18 billion or $20 billion of revenue, and we have no alternative. We will just borrow some more. No problem. Perhaps by the end of the decade we will reach the point when every cent of government revenue will have to go to pay interest on the debt. There will not be anything left for the needed programs of government.
That will not matter, because maybe we can put a second mortgage and a third mortgage on the future of this country. That is the bankrupt position of the Liberals. It has been for the past 20 years. That kind of approach saddled us with a massive national debt. The interest charges on that debt are crippling the ability of the nation today and they offer more of the same.
I find that the position put by the hon. member in this private member's motion is certainly out of touch with reality. I was amazed when, and I believe I am quoting him correctly; he chastised this government for lacking the political courage and honesty to reflect what people want.
What an amazing statement, because time and time again people have indicated that they want to see the deficit dealt with. They view that as the number one

June 12, 1991
Private Members' Business
problem in the country. They want that deficit brought down and they want it eliminated.
How on earth can you do that? How can you reduce the deficit unless you take in more revenue on the one side and either hold or cut spending on the other? Clearly those are the alternatives.
The answer from the hon. member and his party opposite is: "Well, no tax increases." He is going to get rid of the GST, put nothing in its place, lose $18 billion or $20 billion worth of revenue and at the same time, day after day in this House, he and his party oppose every single government proposal to reduce spending.
It seems to me that if we are talking about having the political courage and honesty to face up to the problem, the debt which the Liberal Party created during the Trudeau years and the interest which has to be paid on it, we have to cut spending on the one side and take in more revenue on the other. There is no alternative to it.
The only fleeting or passing alternative is to continue to borrow. That is the Liberal way. You just continue to mortgage tomorrow to pay for today's programs. That is out. I think everyone in the country realizes that is not on anymore.
It is pretty clear to most people that the GST had to come forward. It would be nothing less than irresponsible to consider removing the GST at this point. The amazing thing is to offer nothing in its place. That is incredible. Canada waited for 50 years for sales tax reform. Members opposite and everyone in this House knows that sales tax reform was first proposed back in, I believe, 1940 by the Rowell-Sirois commission. The federal manufacturers' sales tax at that time had been in place for about 15 years. Even then, 50 years ago, it was obvious that it penalized Canadian manufacturers and created problems in that sector. So it was recommended that there be changes.
Subsequent commissions, inquiries and experts for 50 years recommended that something be done. Successive governments looked at this thing and occasionally they came to the brink. The Liberal Party, the Liberal government of those days came to the brink a few times, but lacking the political courage and honesty which the hon. member proposed this motion talks about, it would back off and resort instead to the easy way of borrowing.
Just borrow some more and put out the programs for people. We will not face them with the necessary tax measures in order to pay the bills. No, no, we will
borrow. We will mortgage tomorrow to pay for these programs today.
That is the tragedy. That is why our government finally came forward, faced the facts and accepted the recommendations that have been suggested for over half a century, fell in line with modem society, with 48 other nations, with 19 out of 24 of our partners in the OECD and with most of the industrialized nations of the world and introduced a value added form of sales tax to replace the antiquated tax that we had.
Time will show that this was the appropriate measure. It will expand Canada's manufacturing base. It will expand Canada's industrial capability. It will expand Canada's exports and it will place our manufacturers on a level playing field with their competition. Canada depends on world trade.
I see that you are indicating that my time is almost up, Mr. Speaker. I just want to finish by saying that Canada depends very much on world trade. One out of every three jobs in this country depends on it. This is but one of a number of steps, including liberalized trade negotiations with other nations and with the United States, that we have embarked upon in an effort to to have a more competitive approach for our country leading to more employment for Canadians and a better future for our kids. That is what the GST is all about.
