speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think we have advised the Chair that I will be splitting the 10 minutes that we have allotted with my hon. colleague from Winnipeg.
May I begin by congratulating my colleague for bringing forward this motion. In the five short minutes that I have I want to make a few points, but I cannot begin without at least responding briefly to some of the comments that were made by my friends opposite.
I want to deal not with fiction, not with fantasy, not with fairy tales, but with facts.
The hon. parliamentary secretary had the audacity to say that this government has brought in fair taxation. In my view that is not a fact.
It is a fact that there have been at least 33 separate tax increases since 1984. It is a fact that the average middle income person in this country is presently paying approximately $1,500 a year more in tax than they were in 1984. It is a fact that, during that period of time, while the middle income Canadian has been paying more tax, the high income Canadian has been paying less tax. That, in
June 12, 1991

my view and I would suggest in the view of many Canadians, is not fair taxation.
The parliamentary secretary indicated that there was a major problem with our exporters because of the manufacturers' sales tax. That is also not a fact.
The fact is that exports and exporters were exempted from the manufacturers' sales tax for the most part, except for fixed assets. This was a fiction in effect brought in to justify the scrapping of the manufacturers' sales tax. There is no question the manufacturers' sales tax needed revision, no doubt about that. Let us talk about facts and not about fantasy.
The hon. parliamentary secretary said that the hardware stores in Trois-Rivieres immediately started to reduce their prices on January 1. I was not there, but I can tell the hon. member that I was in Prince Albert at approximately that time. I was told by not one, but two hardware store owners that they had absolutely no intention whatsoever of going through 10,000 items in their hardware stores and changing the prices, despite the fact that they would not have to pay the manufacturers' sales tax and would get an exemption. In fact, their prices did not go down. They may have remained the same, but they did not go down.
I have a great deal of difficulty in believing that if that is what occurred in Prince Albert, it did not occur in Trois-Rivieres.
What about the effects of the goods and services tax? There is no doubt whatsoever that the government did not anticipate a lot of the problems that the goods and services tax introduced.
I want to raise one of them. It is that the goods and services tax was not supposed to tax necessary items, but if there is one thing that is necessary-and I raise this in all sincerity-it is feminine hygiene products. They are not a luxury. They are a necessity and this government chose to tax them. That is an abomination. When I was official opposition critic for revenue I got many letters from constituents and from female Canadians across this country complaining about this. Members on that side have brought this to the government's attention. So far I have not heard an iota of sympathy for female Canadians. It does not care.
What about the rest of the goods and services tax? The proposition was that the goods and services tax would
Private Members' Business
reduce the debt. That is also nonsense because when the goods and services tax was brought in, there was not a word about a debt reduction fund. In all of the previous budgets that the Minister of Finance had, there was not a word about the debt reduction fund. But the government finally realized what a cash cow the goods and services tax would be. It knew that Canadians were up in arms to the tune of 80 per cent to 85 per cent against the services tax, so it said: "Oh, oh, we had better do something", and it came up with this so-called debt reduction fund.
How do I know this? How do I know that this was a last minute thing? Because I got a letter today from the Minister of Supply and Services suggesting that we as members of Parliament respond to our constituents in a certain way. The first thing he says is: "What about the debt reduction fund?" He admits that it was mentioned in the February budget of 1991 and the legislation is not ready yet.
Of course it is not ready yet because it was not even thought of until the last minute to try and save this government from absolute and certain defeat at the polls on this issue and many other issues.
Let us talk about facts and let us not talk about fiction. There is no question that everybody wants the debt reduced, and I for one applaud that if we are going to have this onerous tax, totally contrary to the will of Canadians, at least we should have a debt reduction fund and it should go to reduce the debt, not go into the consolidated revenue fund to be spent by this government any way it sees fit. At least I applaud that much for this government.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   THE CANADIAN ECONOMY REMOVAL OF THE GST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope I get my full five minutes.
I want to say at the outset that this is a timely bill and a timely debate. I want to thank my hon. colleague for Gatineau-La Lievre for bringing forward the bill. I congratulate him on a fine presentation.
The goods and services tax is a very cruel measure. Consider when it was brought in, at a time of high taxation. We all know about this government imposing something like 33 tax increases since it came to power in 1984. We all know that since 1984, since the Conservative government came to power, that the income tax burden, the income tax load on the middle class has gone up $1,500 per family. That is why it is a cruel measure and

June 12, 1991
Private Members' Business
that is why people are as mad as hell and they are not going to.take it any more, to use a well-known cliche.
Another reason why this tax measure is cruel is because when it was brought in, it could not have been brought in at a worse time. It was at a time when the economy was going down and into a recession. Despite all the warnings from us, despite all the warnings from Canadians, the government went ahead and imposed this goods and services tax. That is how much it listened to Canadians and that is how much it is out of tune and out touch with Canadians. This is why I say it was a cruel, cruel measure.
The other thing, and this is why Canadians are so mad, is they feel that they have been had and that they have been betrayed. The Conservative members went around and said first of all that it was going to be neutral and then it was going to get a little bit of extra money but not a whole lot, and if there was some extra money, they would decide later what to do with it.
We hear the story that tracking shows they are getting something like $400 million more in the first quarter than expected and anticipated. The finance minister has the unmitigated gall to say that he is surprised. Tell me another one. If you can believe that, you can believe anything. It is not surprised. It knew in advance that it was going to get that kind of money. It knew in advance that it was an absolute cash cow.
Canadians are upset because the Conservatives promised us tax reform. Back in 1984, they promised us tax reform, and what did we get? All we got were tax forms that are even more complicated, not less complicated and higher taxes. That is an example of tax reform.
Let me just finish on a positive note. I cannot stand here and not offer some kind of alternative to the GST. This GST is not working. It is cruel, and Canadians want it to go.
We do have to look at the taxation system. People are very upset. They are paying too much. They are voting with their feet right now. That is why they are going to the border states. That is why they are crossing the boundary line.
Every time they go across the boundary line into the United States and buy something, they are telling those guys over there that taxes are too high, that the tax system in this country has to be overhauled.
I believe to my very core that the tax system in this country has to be overhauled. It has to be made more equitable. It has to be made more fair.
That is a pledge I make, and I think I can speak very fairly on behalf of everybody on this side. We know that the tax system is not fair. It must be overhauled. By golly, we are committed to it.
This tax is unfair. Canadians do not want it. They are telling Conservatives that over and over. Not only are they telling them with their feet as they go across the border to buy goods in the States, but they are also telling the Conservatives in the polls.
That is why they are down at 14 per cent. That is why they are going down to 10 per cent. Maybe they will even go out of sight. It is because of this dam tax system that they are using to beat us over the head.
